title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text:
1 Background

Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have 
    P(X \le x) = F_X(x) = P(U \le F_X(x)) = P(F_X^{-1}(U) \le x).
 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Sample the points
N = 10000
inv_cdf = lambda x: np.sqrt(x)
R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)
plt.xticks([])
plt.yticks([])
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Sampling 10000 points uniformly on the unit disk.

Try it. Pluck the string, then pick a point to touch and pluck again. String players call these notes harmonics.
And here is a whole violin to play: press and hold a string, slide to finger it, and choose the bow or plucking.
To explain the harmonics, we need to know what a string’s ends do to the circle’s operator.

title: 4 · A string with ends
text:
Tie the ends down
The operator and its boundary condition. A string of length L, tension T and mass \mu per unit length obeys the wave equation, derived on the circle page: 
u_{tt} = -c^2 A u, \qquad A = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \qquad u(0) = u(L) = 0 .
 The same rule -d^2/dx^2 now acts on shapes on the interval [0, L], and only shapes that vanish at both ends are allowed. That restriction, called a Dirichlet condition, changes which shapes are eigenfunctions, and so changes the spectrum. An operator is the rule together with the shapes it is allowed to act on. As on the circle page, the operator proper is c^2A, and we work with A.
Spectrum. The solutions of -X'' = k^2X are a\cos kx + b\sin kx. The condition X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 then needs \sin kL = 0, so k = n\pi/L. The eigenfunctions are \sin(n\pi x/L) for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with eigenvalues (n\pi/L)^2, and the frequencies are 
f_n = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi} = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} .
 Exactly whole-number multiples of f_1, as on the circle. (There are no other eigenvalues. Multiply -X'' = \lambda X by X and integrate by parts, using X = 0 at both ends: \lambda\int X^2\,dx = \int (X')^2\,dx. So a zero or negative \lambda would need \int (X')^2\,dx \le 0, which only X = 0 satisfies.) Each eigenvalue now has multiplicity 1, not 2: a wave running along the string reflects at the ends instead of going around, and each reflected pair forms one standing wave.



ProofThe string is half of a circle: the sine series as a Fourier series uses Fourier series and the uniqueness of solutions of the wave equation

Take a shape u on [0, L] with u(0) = u(L) = 0. Extend it to [-L, 0] by u(-x) = -u(x), an odd reflection, and then repeat with period 2L. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 2L.

  
  
  
  
  0L−L
  stringodd reflection


Odd shapes stay odd. If u(x, t) solves the wave equation on the loop, so does -u(-x, t), since two derivatives in x do not change sign under x \mapsto -x. Starting from an odd shape at rest, both are the same solution by uniqueness, so the motion stays odd.
Odd shapes on the loop are exactly string shapes. An odd periodic shape vanishes at 0, because u(0) = -u(0), and at L, because u(L) = u(-L) = -u(L). Conversely every string shape extends this way.
So the string’s eigenfunctions are the loop’s odd eigenfunctions. On a loop of circumference 2L the eigenfunctions are \cos(n\pi x/L) and \sin(n\pi x/L) with eigenvalues (n\pi/L)^2. The odd ones are the sines. Each eigenvalue keeps one of its two eigenfunctions, which is why the multiplicity drops from 2 to 1.

The sine series of a string shape, u = \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L), is therefore the Fourier series of its odd extension, and everything proved on the circle page carries over. The same trick with an even reflection, u(-x) = u(x), gives the cosines and the condition u'(0) = u'(L) = 0; the next page combines both reflections for air in a tube.





Step-by-step derivationThe same result from beads with the ends tied uses matrices, as on page 2

Put N beads of mass m, spaced h apart, on a thread of tension T, with both ends tied, so u_0 = u_{N+1} = 0. The force on bead j is the one derived on the ring page, so m\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}). The matrix is now the ring’s matrix without its two corner entries: 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & & \\ -1 & 2 & \ddots & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & -1\\ & & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Its eigenvectors are v_j = \sin\big(n\pi j/(N+1)\big), the sampled sines, with eigenvalues 4\sin^2\big(n\pi/(2(N+1))\big) for n = 1, \dots, N. To check: \sin(\alpha(j+1)) + \sin(\alpha(j-1)) = 2\cos\alpha\,\sin(\alpha j), so (Kv)_j = (2 - 2\cos\alpha)\,v_j = 4\sin^2(\alpha/2)\,v_j with \alpha = n\pi/(N+1), and the tied ends hold because \sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0. As on the ring, letting N \to \infty with L = (N+1)h and \mu = m/h fixed gives the wave equation and the frequencies f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}.

title: 4 · A string with ends
section: The finger and the still points
text:
The finger and the still points
Let the finger touch the string at the distance s from the nut, and write X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L) for the shape of mode n. A light touch is a soft contact that soaks up energy: it barely changes the modes, but it drains each one in proportion to how much that mode moves under the finger, roughly X_n(s)^2. The piano page derives this rule for the piano’s felt dampers; for a finger it is a rough guide, not an exact law. The modes that survive are the ones with a node, a point that never moves, right under the finger: \sin(n\pi s/L) = 0, which means ns/L is a whole number. At the middle, s = L/2, the surviving modes are the even ones, at 2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots: a note with fundamental 2f_1, an octave up. At s = L/3 they are n = 3, 6, 9, \dots, with fundamental 3f_1: an octave (a factor 2) and a fifth (a factor 3/2) up, since 2 \times 3/2 = 3. Pressing the string down firmly is different, as described under Fingers below.

title: 4 · A string with ends
text:
Where you pluck
By the circle page, every shape of the string is a sum \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L) of its modes, and b_n says how much of mode n the shape contains. A string pulled aside a distance d at a point x_p from one end, and let go, starts as a triangle. With x_p measured from the nut, where x = 0, its sine coefficients are 
b_n = \frac{2dL^2}{\pi^2 x_p(L - x_p)}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi x_p/L)}{n^2}.
 Measuring x_p from the bridge instead only flips the sign of every second b_n, since \sin(n\pi(L - x_p)/L) = \pm\sin(n\pi x_p/L), and signs do not change how loud a mode is; from here on x_p is the distance from the bridge. What reaches your ear is driven by the force on the bridge, which is proportional to the string’s slope there and so to n\,b_n for mode n. Near the bridge, x_p small, \sin(n\pi x_p/L) \approx n\pi x_p/L for the first several modes, so n b_n hardly falls off at all: the high modes are strong and the sound is bright. At the middle, \sin(n\pi/2) is zero for every even n, and the rest have n b_n falling like 1/n: a mellower, hollow sound.



Step-by-step derivationThe sine coefficients of a plucked string uses integration by parts

Take L = 1 and write q = x_p. The starting shape is u_0(x) = dx/q for 0 \le x \le q and u_0(x) = d(1 - x)/(1 - q) for q \le x \le 1. Its sine coefficients are b_n = 2\int_0^1 u_0(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx, by the perpendicularity of the sines, which the first fold above inherits from the circle page. Integrate by parts twice on each straight piece. Since u_0 vanishes at both ends and u_0'' = 0 on each piece, the only term left comes from the jump in slope at the corner, from d/q just left of it to -d/(1-q) just right of it: b_n = \frac{2}{n^2\pi^2}\big(\tfrac{d}{q} + \tfrac{d}{1-q}\big)\sin(n\pi q) = \frac{2d\sin(n\pi q)}{n^2\pi^2 q(1-q)}. The 1/n^2 comes from that single corner.


Fingers. The nut is the end of the string near the tuning pegs, and an open string is one not pressed down by a finger. A finger pressed firmly onto the fingerboard makes a new tied end, and the piece between the finger and the bridge sounds on its own. With the finger at distance s from the nut, the vibrating length shrinks to L - s, so the pitch rises by the factor L/(L - s). In equal temperament the twelve semitones of an octave are equal ratios of frequency, so each is 2^{1/12}, and k semitones are 2^{k/12}. Solving L/(L - s) = 2^{k/12} gives s_k = (1 - 2^{-k/12})L: the semitone positions bunch together toward the bridge.
The bow. The bow grips the string and drags it along until the string’s pull tears it free; it slips back, and is gripped again. Hermann von Helmholtz watched it with a vibration microscope, whose lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion, and reported it in 1860 and in his 1863 book: the string forms two straight pieces joined by one sharp corner, and the corner races back and forth between the bridge and the finger, once per period. This is called Helmholtz motion. Its expansion in the string’s eigenfunctions is, for some overall size a, 
u(x,t) = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(2\pi n f_1 t).
 Where this comes from: at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at some point x_c. Helmholtz showed that the corner’s height is proportional to x_c(L - x_c), so it traces two arcs of a parabola, the lens in the demo, and that the corner moves at the wave speed c = 2Lf_1. Put that height in place of d in the pluck formula above: the factor x_c(L - x_c) cancels and b_n \propto \sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2. With x_c = 2Lf_1t this is \sin(2\pi nf_1t)/n^2; on the way back the corner runs along the lower arc, and the same formula covers it: for x_c between L and 2L, \sin(n\pi x_c/L) describes a corner at 2L - x_c with negative height. The motion repeats exactly every 1/f_1 seconds, so its partials sit exactly on nf_1. The force on the bridge is proportional to the string’s slope there, and the slope of \sin(n\pi x/L) carries an extra factor n\pi/L, so partial n pushes the bridge with strength proportional to 1/n. On an ideal string a pluck also gives exact multiples of f_1. The difference shows on a real string, which is slightly stiff, so its own frequencies run a little sharp of the whole numbers (page 7): plucked, each mode rings at its own slightly sharp frequency and fades; bowed, the stick and slip lock the whole motion into exact repetition. That locking is a property of the bow’s friction, which is not linear, and is observed rather than derived here.


    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens-shaped outline is the path the corner traces. Stems: partials of the bridge force.
  

The body. The string itself moves very little air. It rocks the bridge, the bridge shakes the wooden body, and the body moves the air. Each step is linear, and a linear system shaken at one frequency responds at that same frequency, only scaled and delayed. So the body can make each partial louder or quieter but can never move it to another frequency. Toggle the wooden body in the first demo: the stems change height and stay where they are.

A boundary condition, the rule for what the ends of the string may do, is part of the operator. Tying the ends down keeps the circle’s operator but keeps only half of its eigenfunctions, the sines, so the frequencies are still exactly whole-number multiples. A light touch drains every mode that moves under the finger, so only the modes that already have a still point there survive.

The next puzzle
A flute and a clarinet are both tubes of air, and about the same length. Yet the clarinet’s lowest note is almost an octave below the flute’s, and when the players overblow, making the tube jump to its next mode, the flute jumps up an octave while the clarinet jumps an octave and a fifth. The same operator governs the air in both. What is different?

title: 9 · What the spectrum knows
section: What a list of frequencies can tell you
text:
What a list of frequencies can tell you
The question. A drum’s operator, from the drum page, is -c^2\Delta on the drumhead \Omega, a bounded region of the plane in one piece, with u = 0 on the rim. Here \Delta is the Laplacian. Write \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \lambda_3 \le \cdots for the eigenvalues of -\Delta, each repeated as many times as it occurs (its multiplicity). The drum’s frequencies are then f_k = \frac{c}{2\pi}\sqrt{\lambda_k}. Kac’s question, in these terms, is whether the list \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots determines the shape of \Omega.
What can be heard: area and perimeter. Count the eigenvalues up to \lambda: N(\lambda) = \#\{k : \lambda_k \le \lambda\}, where \# means “the number of”. For large \lambda, 
N(\lambda) \approx \frac{A}{4\pi}\,\lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\lambda},
 where A is the area of the drum and P the length of its rim, and “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\lambda, shrinks to zero as \lambda grows. The first term is Weyl’s law. Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum. So the area can be heard: it is 4\pi times the rate at which N grows.
The second term is subtler. Weyl conjectured it, and Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for drums with smooth rims, provided that closed billiard paths are rare. A billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved. The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the first fold below. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the second fold.
So from the list of frequencies alone one can recover the area and the perimeter. The demo counts the eigenvalues of three drums with the same area.


  
  
    Count N(λ)
    Count minus the area term
  
  Up to λ =
  
  Three drums, each of area π: a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide. Steps: the true counts, computed from the exact eigenvalues. Dashed: Weyl's two-term formula. Gray: the area term λ/4 alone, shared by all three. Subtracting it leaves roughly −P√λ/4π, so the longer rim gives the lower curve.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the circle on page 3. So N(\lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\lambda = \frac{A}{4\pi}\lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of any drum: a smoother count uses the heat equation and the reflection trick of page 4

N(\lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if \lambda_k is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-\lambda_k t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_k^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode k in proportion to X_k(x), the same rule as a strike on the drum page; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-\lambda_k t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_k(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}X_k(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives A/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim, the odd reflection of the string page. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{A}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off A from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper. Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method; Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured, from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim; and Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988. Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


A drum you can hear: the disk. Of all shapes with a given area, the disk has the shortest rim: P^2 \ge 4\pi A, with equality only for the disk. This is the isoperimetric inequality. Both sides can be heard. So a drum, with a smooth or polygonal rim, that has exactly the frequencies of a disk has the disk’s area and perimeter, so P^2 = 4\pi A, so it is a disk. Kac pointed this out in his 1966 paper (section 10): “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!” Some shapes, then, can be heard.
What cannot be heard. For shapes without a rim the answer was already known to be no, at least in 16 dimensions, and Kac said so: two years before his paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same spectrum in 16 dimensions, two flat tori, the 16-dimensional version of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left. Whether this could happen in the plane stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert answered Kac’s question: no. They found two different polygons whose operators have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, the two drums at the top of this page. Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and perimeter can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven right triangles with two short sides of length 1, so the area is 3.5, and each has perimeter 6 + 3\sqrt2.



Why it worksTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other uses the Laplacian (page 8)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with eigenvalue \lambda. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = \lambda X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same \lambda. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992; the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler. The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post on transplantation, and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada from 1985 for building isospectral spaces from group theory; Wikipedia has an overview.





MethodHow the numbers on this page were computed uses matrices, as on page 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of page 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way. Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these. That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives the eigenvalue \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post. The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.


Same frequencies, not the same sound. A struck drum’s sound is a sum of its modes, each at its own frequency and with a strength that depends on where it is struck and where it is heard. The two drums share the frequencies. The mode shapes differ, so the strengths from a strike at a given point differ, and so does the timbre. What the drums share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly the spectrum.

title: 9 · What the spectrum knows
text:
What we found
The list of a drum’s frequencies determines the drum’s area and its perimeter, and for a disk that is enough to pin down the shape. In general it is not: two differently shaped drums can have exactly the same list. Looking back, every page has used two ideas: an instrument’s frequencies are the spectrum of an operator, and a clear pitch means the frequencies you hear sit at or near whole-number multiples of one frequency. This page asked the reverse question, what the spectrum says about the instrument; the study of such questions is called spectral geometry.

The demo starts with one bead plucked; watch the tangle. Then press the mode buttons one at a time. In each mode, every bead swings at the same frequency and the overall shape never changes, and the tangle is all of the modes at once. In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle.

title: 2 · Beads on a ring
text:
Untangling the motion
The force on one bead. Let u_j be the height of bead j, with beads spaced h apart along a string of tension T, each of mass m. Because the loop closes, bead N is next to bead 1, so indices are counted around the ring. (This is an idealization: a real loop of string would need something to hold it out against its own tension. The model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, exactly as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.) For small displacements, Newton’s law for bead j is 
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).




Step-by-step derivationWhy the force is the difference between a bead and its neighbors


  
  
  
  
  
  bead j−1bead jbead j+1
  TTnet pull


The string between beads j and j+1 pulls bead j along itself with force T.
Its slope is (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h. Let \theta be the angle that piece of string makes with the horizontal. For small slopes the vertical part of the pull is T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T(u_{j+1} - u_j)/h.
The string on the other side contributes T(u_{j-1} - u_j)/h.
Adding the two and applying Newton’s law gives the equation above. The bracket u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1} is twice the gap between the average of the neighbors and bead j itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up.

The assumptions are small slopes and a tension that does not change as the string flexes.


The matrix. Collect the heights into a column u = (u_1, \dots, u_N). The equations for all beads at once read \ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K u, where K is the N\times N matrix with 2 on the diagonal, -1 just above and below it, and -1 in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead N are neighbors. For N = 5, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Here Ku is the column whose j-th entry is row j of K times u: multiply each entry of row j by the matching entry of u, and add. Row j has 2 in place j and -1 in places j - 1 and j + 1, so (Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}, and the matrix equation is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of K is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called circulant.
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. A nonzero column v is an eigenvector of K, with eigenvalue \lambda, if Kv = \lambda v: the matrix only rescales it, possibly by zero. The set of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of K.
Modes. If Kv = \lambda v, then u(t) = v\cos(\omega t) is a motion of the beads, provided \omega^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda. To check, differentiate twice: \ddot u = -\omega^2 v\cos\omega t, while -\frac{T}{mh}Ku = -\frac{T}{mh}\lambda v\cos\omega t. Every bead swings at the same angular frequency \omega (radians per second; page 1), in the fixed shape v. This is the mass on a spring again, once for each eigenvector.
A small example, three beads. For N = 3, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Row j of this K gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j - (v_1 + v_2 + v_3). The column (1, 1, 1) gives K(1,1,1) = (0,0,0), so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0: every bead moves up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts. Any column whose entries add up to zero gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j, so Kv = 3v. Every such column is a combination a(1, -1, 0) + b(0, 1, -1), so these eigenvectors fill a whole plane: every one is built from those two shapes, and neither of the two is a multiple of the other. The eigenvalues are 0, 3, 3, with 3 counted twice: it has multiplicity 2.
Any number of beads. Try the column v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N), a wave with k crests around the ring. The identity \cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b, with a = 2\pi jk/N and b = 2\pi k/N, gives v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j, so 
(Kv)_j = 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} = \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j = 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
 using 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x. The same holds for v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N). These are the shapes the mode buttons play, and the eigenvalues are 4\sin^2(\pi k/N). At the beads, a wave with N - k crests looks exactly like one with k crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from k = 0, 1, \dots up to N/2, rounded down, and each one from k = 1 up to just below N/2 has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At k = 0, and at k = N/2 when N is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) Writing any motion as a sum of these waves splits it into separate masses on springs, one per wave; that splitting is the discrete Fourier transform.



Complex formThe same waves as e^{2\pi i jk/N} uses complex numbers

With Euler’s formula e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x, the cosine and sine waves combine into v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N} for k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 (here i is the imaginary unit and j the bead number). Then (Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j in one line. These N waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor e^{\mp i\omega t}, the waves with k and N - k crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.


Not quite whole numbers. The frequencies are proportional to \sin(\pi k/N), which is not proportional to k, so the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small k, \sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N, so the low modes are nearly harmonic: raise N in the demo and watch the low stems approach the whole-number grid. The modes near k = N/2 stay far from it.



ProofEvery motion is a sum of modes uses linear algebra

The matrix K is symmetric: the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. By the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, K has a basis of N mutually orthogonal (perpendicular) eigenvectors v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(N)} with real eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N. Write the motion as u(t) = \sum_k a_k(t)\,v^{(k)}. Substituting into \ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}Ku and taking the dot product with v^{(k)}, which removes every other term because they are perpendicular, gives \ddot a_k = -\omega_k^2 a_k with \omega_k^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda_k: each coefficient obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation. With starting shape u(0) = \sum_k c_k v^{(k)} and starting velocity \dot u(0) = \sum_k d_k v^{(k)}, and by the uniqueness of solutions from page 1, every motion is u(t) = \sum_k \big(c_k\cos\omega_k t + \frac{d_k}{\omega_k}\sin\omega_k t\big)v^{(k)}, read as c_k + d_k t when \omega_k = 0. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0, by regrouping the terms around the ring; for an eigenvector this equals \lambda\,(u\cdot u).

title: 2 · Beads on a ring
text:
What we found
Many coupled masses move in a few special shapes, called modes, each swinging at its own frequency. Finding them means finding the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a matrix, the operator \frac{T}{mh}K, whose list of eigenvalues, its spectrum, gives the frequencies. On a ring, the modes are exactly the waves of the discrete Fourier transform.

The second question has a history. From the 1740s on, Jean d’Alembert, Leonhard Euler and Daniel Bernoulli all worked on the vibrating string. D’Alembert showed in 1747 that a string can move in essentially any smooth shape. Bernoulli held that every vibration is a sum of simple modes, which for a string are sine-shaped. Euler objected that a sum of sines could not represent an arbitrary shape, such as a string plucked into a sharp corner, and d’Alembert doubted that such a sum was physical at all. The argument went on for decades. This page answers the first question, and then the second.

title: 3 · The circle
text:
Why exactly whole numbers
From beads to a loop. Measure position around the loop by the angle \theta, and choose units so that the loop has circumference 2\pi. Bead j sits at \theta_j = jh with h = 2\pi/N. Let \mu be the mass per unit length, so each bead has mass m = \mu h, and write u(\theta, t) for the height of the loop at angle \theta and time t, so that u_j(t) = u(\theta_j, t). Dividing the bead equation from the previous page by m gives 
\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{\mu}\cdot\frac{u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}}{h^2}.
 The fraction on the right has a simple meaning. (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h is the slope of the string just to the right of bead j, and (u_j - u_{j-1})/h the slope just to the left. Their difference, divided by h once more, measures how fast the slope changes: the second derivative. So as the beads crowd together, h \to 0, the bead equation becomes 
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}.
 Here u depends on two things, the angle and the time. The symbol \partial u/\partial t, a partial derivative, is the derivative in time with the angle held fixed, and \partial u/\partial\theta the derivative in angle with the time held fixed; the second derivatives are also written u_{tt} and u_{\theta\theta}. This is the wave equation. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels around the loop; the second demo shows it.



Step-by-step derivationWhy the second difference becomes the second derivative uses Taylor’s theorem

Expand the neighbors with Taylor’s theorem, assuming the shape has four continuous derivatives: 
u(\theta \pm h) = u \pm h\,u' + \tfrac{h^2}{2}u'' \pm \tfrac{h^3}{6}u''' + O(h^4),
 where O(h^4) stands for terms no bigger than a constant times h^4. Add the two expansions and subtract 2u. The odd terms cancel in pairs: 
u(\theta + h) - 2u(\theta) + u(\theta - h) = h^2 u''(\theta) + O(h^4).
 Divide by h^2: the fraction equals u'' + O(h^2), which tends to u''. What was held fixed: the circumference, the tension T, and the mass per length \mu. So as the beads multiply, each one gets lighter in proportion.

The middle bead sits above the average of its neighbors by about -\tfrac{h^2}{2}u'', which is positive where the curve bends down (u'' < 0). That is why the force on a bead, and so its acceleration, is proportional to the curvature u''.


The operator. Write the wave equation as 
u_{tt} = -c^2 A u, \qquad A = -\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}.
 The operator A takes a shape f(\theta) and returns a new shape, -f''. Strictly, the operator in the sense of the series page, minus the restoring force per unit mass, is c^2A; the constant c^2 only scales the eigenvalues, so this page works with A and puts c back in the frequencies. The minus sign is a convention that makes A of a bump positive at the bump; the restoring force per unit mass is -c^2 Af, which pulls the bump back down. If you read page 2, A is the continuous version of the beads’ matrix K/h^2.
Which shapes. A shape on the loop is a function f(\theta) that returns to itself after one turn: f(\theta + 2\pi) = f(\theta).
Eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. An eigenfunction of A is a shape that A only rescales: Af = \lambda f for some number \lambda, called the eigenvalue. Try \cos n\theta, a wave with n crests around the loop. Its second derivative is -n^2\cos n\theta, so 
A\cos n\theta = n^2\cos n\theta, \qquad A\sin n\theta = n^2\sin n\theta .
 These shapes close up after one turn exactly when n is a whole number. So the spectrum of A, the list of its eigenvalues, is 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, \dots Each n^2 with n \ge 1 belongs to two eigenfunctions, \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta, which are the same wave shifted by a quarter of a wavelength; n = 0 belongs to the constant shape, the whole loop lifted at once. The first fold below proves that there are no other eigenvalues.
Frequencies. The shape \cos(n\theta)\cos(\omega t) solves the wave equation when \omega^2 = c^2 n^2: differentiate it twice in t and twice in \theta and compare. Here \omega is the angular frequency, in radians per second, and the frequency in hertz is f = \omega/2\pi. So mode n sounds at f_n = cn/2\pi, exactly n times the lowest. (In ordinary units, for a loop of circumference \ell, this is f_n = nc/\ell: the time for a bump to travel once around, \ell/c, is the period of the lowest mode.) The eigenvalues are perfect squares; the frequencies, proportional to their square roots, are whole-number multiples of one frequency. The ring of beads approaches this from below:

Frequency of mode k divided by the frequency of mode 1. On the ring of N beads the ratio is \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N).

ProofThe eigenvalues are exactly 0, 1, 4, 9, … uses integration by parts

Step 1: no eigenvalue is negative. For periodic shapes f and g, integrate by parts twice. The boundary terms are values at \theta = 2\pi minus values at \theta = 0, which cancel because the shapes are periodic: 
\int_0^{2\pi} (Af)\,g\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} f''g\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} f'g'\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} f g''\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,(Ag)\,d\theta .
 An operator with this property is called symmetric, by analogy with a symmetric matrix. (With the right choice of allowed shapes it is also self-adjoint, the stronger property that the spectral theorem in the fold below needs.) If Af = \lambda f with f not identically zero, take g = f in the middle expression: \lambda\int_0^{2\pi} f^2\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}(f')^2\,d\theta \ge 0, so \lambda \ge 0. (For a complex-valued f, use \int f\bar f\,d\theta = \int |f|^2\,d\theta instead, as in the complex-form fold below; the same computation shows that \lambda is real and at least 0.)
Step 2: solve the equation. Af = \lambda f means f'' = -\lambda f.

If \lambda = 0, then f = a + b\theta, which returns to itself after one turn only when b = 0. Eigenvalue 0, eigenfunctions the constants.
If \lambda > 0, write \lambda = s^2 with s > 0; then f = a\cos s\theta + b\sin s\theta, a wave that repeats every 2\pi/s radians. It returns to itself after one full turn exactly when 2\pi is a whole number of these periods, that is, when s is a whole number n. Eigenvalue n^2, eigenfunctions \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta.

Step 3: eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues are perpendicular, in the sense used below: \int_0^{2\pi} \cos n\theta\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for n \ne m, and similarly for sines and for a sine against a cosine. This can be checked directly with the product formulas for cosines, and it also follows from Step 1, just as for a symmetric matrix.
For readers who know functional analysis: A is not defined on every square-integrable function, only on those with two derivatives in L^2, the Sobolev space H^2(S^1). On that domain it is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric: in Fourier coefficients it is multiplication by n^2 on the sequences with \sum n^4|c_n|^2 < \infty. That there is no spectrum besides these eigenvalues follows from the completeness of the eigenfunctions, the Theorem fold below.

title: 3 · The circle
text:
Who was right
Bernoulli, in a sense that took mathematicians more than a century to make precise. Every shape of the loop, corners included, is a sum of the operator’s eigenfunctions. Euler’s worry was reasonable, since every sine is smooth and a corner is not, but an infinite sum of smooth waves need not be smooth.
The Fourier series is the eigenfunction expansion. With the beads we wrote the starting shape as a sum of eigenvectors and let each one swing on its own. Here the same move reads 
f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big),
 the Fourier series of f. To find the numbers a_n and b_n, use the fact that the eigenfunctions are perpendicular. For whole numbers n \ne m, 
\int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, \qquad \int_0^{2\pi}\sin n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0,
 while \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for all n and m, and \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \pi for n \ge 1. To check them, turn each product into a sum with \cos A\cos B = \tfrac12[\cos(A - B) + \cos(A + B)] and its relatives for sines; every cosine or sine of a nonzero whole-number multiple of \theta integrates to zero over a full turn. These integrals are the continuous version of the dot product: for two columns of bead heights, \sum_j u_j v_j\,h is a dot product times h, and as the beads crowd together it becomes \int f g\,d\theta. Now multiply both sides of the series by \cos m\theta and integrate from 0 to 2\pi. Every term drops out except the one with n = m, which leaves \pi a_m. So 
a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\cos n\theta\,d\theta, \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\sin n\theta\,d\theta,
 just as a vector’s component along an axis is its dot product with that axis. The constant term is written a_0/2 so that the same formula also gives a_0: for n = 0, \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 0\,d\theta = 2\pi, not \pi. Released from rest in the shape f, each eigenfunction swings at its own frequency: 
u(\theta, t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big)\cos(c\,n\,t).
 Every term returns to its starting value after the time 2\pi/c, so the whole motion repeats, and any sound it makes has a pitch. The demo below builds a plucked shape, corner and all, out of cosines and lets it go. The folds below give the same series in complex notation and state the theorem that settles the old argument.


  
  Eigenfunctions used, up to n =
  Let goHear the loop, at the plucked point
  
  The loop is cut open and laid flat: the left and right edges are the same point. Dashed: the plucked shape, and, once released, the exact motion, in which the bump splits into two copies of half the height that travel apart in opposite directions. Solid: the sum of the eigenfunctions cos nθ up to the chosen n, each swinging at its own frequency.





Complex formThe same series with e^{in\theta}, and the space of all shapes uses complex numbers

With Euler’s formula e^{in\theta} = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta, the pair \cos n\theta, \sin n\theta can be traded for the pair e^{in\theta}, e^{-in\theta}, and A e^{in\theta} = n^2 e^{in\theta}. The Fourier series becomes 
f(\theta) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n\,e^{in\theta}, \qquad c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\,e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta ,
 with c_{\pm n} = (a_n \mp i b_n)/2 for n \ge 1 and c_0 = a_0/2. The perpendicularity above becomes \langle e^{in\theta}, e^{im\theta}\rangle = 0 for n \ne m, for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta; the bar, complex conjugation, is what makes \langle f, f\rangle a positive number for complex-valued f. The natural space of shapes is L^2(S^1), all functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite: the shapes of finite “total squared height”.





TheoremEvery shape is a sum of eigenfunctions advanced: uses functional analysis

Statement. The functions e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi}, n \in \mathbb{Z}, form an orthonormal basis of L^2(S^1). That is, for every f in L^2(S^1), 
\Big\| f - \sum_{|n| \le M} c_n e^{in\theta} \Big\| \to 0 \quad (M \to \infty), \qquad \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta = \sum_n |c_n|^2 ,
 the second identity being Parseval’s.
Why it needs a proof. For a symmetric N\times N matrix, N perpendicular eigenvectors automatically span everything, because the space has dimension N. Here there are infinitely many eigenfunctions and the space is infinite-dimensional, so one has to show that no shape is perpendicular to all of them. One standard proof shows that trigonometric sums can approximate any continuous periodic function uniformly (Fejér’s theorem), and that continuous functions are dense in L^2. See Stein and Shakarchi, chapters 2 and 3.
Pointwise. Convergence in L^2 is convergence of the total squared error. At individual points more care is needed: there are continuous functions whose Fourier series diverge at a point. For the shapes on this page, continuous and made of straight pieces, the series converges at every point. The plucked triangle’s coefficients shrink like 1/n^2, which is why a few terms already look right in the demo.
What it took. The old argument could not be settled until “sum” had a precise meaning for infinitely many terms. Fourier claimed such expansions for arbitrary functions in his 1807 work on heat. Dirichlet proved in 1829 that the series converges at every point for a broad class of functions, including shapes with corners; the L^2 statement above belongs to the early 20th century; and that the Fourier series of every L^2 function converges at almost every point was proved only in 1966, by Lennart Carleson (Wikipedia). In the L^2 sense, Bernoulli was right and Euler’s corner is no obstacle.
The pattern for every later page. Each instrument’s operator A will be self-adjoint and nonnegative, and (A + 1)^{-1} will be a compact operator. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators then gives the same three facts as here: a list of real eigenvalues growing to infinity, perpendicular eigenfunctions, and an expansion of every shape in them. Only the list and the shapes change.





Reader questionu'' + k^2u = 0 has a single k. Where does an infinite list of frequencies come from?

In that equation k was chosen in advance, and for each k it has the two solutions \cos k\theta and \sin k\theta. The eigenvalue question runs the other way: for which k does a solution go once around the loop and come back to itself? Every whole number k does, and nothing limits how many times a wave may wind around, so the list never ends. The count matches the number of ways the system can move: N beads have N eigenvalues, counted with repetitions, and a continuous loop has infinitely many.
For readers who know functional analysis: on an infinite straight string, with no loop to close up and no ends, every k \ge 0 gives a bounded wave e^{ikx} and the spectrum is the whole half-line [0, \infty). Strictly, these waves are not eigenfunctions, because \int|e^{ikx}|^2\,dx is infinite. This is one reason the general definition of spectrum is more than a list of eigenvalues. A bounded instrument, closed up or with ends that are not too irregular, has a discrete list.





Reader questionHow is the shape \cos n\theta related to the factor \cos(\omega_n t)?

Both come from separating variables. Look for a motion in which the shape stays fixed and only its size changes: u = X(\theta)\,q(t). Substituting into u_{tt} = c^2u_{\theta\theta} and dividing by Xq gives q''/q = c^2X''/X. The left side depends only on t and the right only on \theta. Changing t alone cannot change the right side, so the left side cannot change either; the same holds the other way round, so both sides equal one constant. That constant cannot be positive, because A has no negative eigenvalues (Step 1 of the proof above), so we call it -\omega^2. That splits the equation in two. In time, q'' = -\omega^2 q, so q = \cos(\omega t + \phi), times any constant: the mass on a spring. (For \omega = 0 the solution is q = a + bt instead: the loop drifts as a whole.) In space, -X'' = (\omega/c)^2 X with X periodic: the eigenvalue problem for A, which allows only \omega/c = n. The space part chooses the frequency, and the time part swings at it. The time factor is a cosine, for every nonzero frequency, for every instrument in this series, because every operator here has no negative eigenvalues and every equation has two time derivatives and no friction term; damping, added on page 7, multiplies the cosine by a decaying factor. Everything instrument-specific lives in the space part.

title: 3 · The circle
text:
What we found
A continuous loop of string has an operator, -\tfrac{d^2}{d\theta^2}, acting on its shapes; it is what the beads’ matrix becomes when they crowd together. Its eigenvalues are exactly 0, 1, 4, 9, \dots, so the frequencies are exactly 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots times a base frequency. Writing a shape as a sum of this operator’s eigenfunctions is the Fourier series. This is the smallest example of an operator’s spectrum: one dimension, no ends, the same string everywhere. Every later page follows the same pattern, with a different operator: a list of eigenvalues that grows without end, eigenfunctions that are perpendicular to one another, and every shape a sum of eigenfunctions. Only the list and the shapes change.

Here is the same trick on a drumhead. Pick a note and watch where the sand goes.
Napoleon offered a prize for a mathematical explanation of Chladni’s patterns. It was won in 1816 by Sophie Germain, the first woman to receive the grand prize in mathematics of the Paris Academy. Her theory had errors, and the Academy was still not fully satisfied with it; Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850. The lines the sand draws are the places where the surface does not move, and finding them is the same kind of problem as finding the frequencies: for a drumhead, the problem on this page; for Chladni’s plates, the same problem with the plate’s own operator.
Now strike the drum itself. Tap the head anywhere below.

title: 8 · The drum
text:
A sheet pulled tight
The operator. A drumhead with tension T, measured as force per unit length of any cut through it, and mass \sigma per unit area obeys 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\sigma}, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on the rim}.
 The operator is -c^2\Delta; \Delta, the Laplacian, adds the second partial derivatives in the two directions across the sheet. On a string, the restoring force was proportional to how far a point sits below the average of its two neighbors; on a sheet it is proportional to how far a point sits below the average of the points around it, and that is what \Delta u measures.


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      patch DT ds
    
    Tension pulls outward all around the edge. Where the sheet bulges, the pulls tilt and their vertical parts add up to T times the Laplacian of u, per unit area.
  




Step-by-step derivationNewton’s law for a patch of drumhead uses multivariable calculus


Take any small patch D of the head. Along each short piece ds of its edge, the sheet outside pulls with force T\,ds, along the surface and outward.
For small slopes the vertical part of that pull is T\,\partial_n u\,ds, where \partial_n u is the slope of the head in the outward direction across the edge. This is the string’s T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta again.
Add these up around the edge. The divergence theorem turns the sum around the edge into a sum over the inside: 
T\oint_{\partial D} \partial_n u\,ds = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA .

Newton’s law for the patch reads \iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA. This holds for every patch, however small, so the integrands are equal at every point: \sigma u_{tt} = T\Delta u.

In one dimension a patch is a segment, its edge is its two endpoints, and step 3 is the fundamental theorem of calculus, u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx. That is the string’s equation again.
What was assumed: small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, and no air. The air matters for real drums, as the note above says.


Spectrum, and the sand’s lines. A mode is a fixed shape X swinging as X\cos\omega t, with -\Delta X = k^2 X where k = \omega/c, and X = 0 on the rim. For a round drum of radius a, measure position by the distance r from the center and the angle \theta. Going once around the drum, a mode must return to itself, so its dependence on the angle is \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta with m a whole number: the loop of page 3, inside the drum. Its dependence on r is a Bessel function, so the modes are 
J_m(k r)\cos m\theta \quad\text{and}\quad J_m(kr)\sin m\theta, \qquad m = 0, 1, 2, \dots
 The Bessel function J_m plays the part that the sine played on a string: it wiggles like a cosine or sine whose swings slowly shrink. Its zeros are not whole-number multiples of the first one: those of J_0 are at 2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654, \dots, in the ratios 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. They are spaced by about \pi, but shifted: the first is about 0.77\pi, not \pi, so the later ones are not multiples of it. J_0 starts at 1 at the center; J_1, J_2, … start at 0.











J₀ (starts at 1)J₁ (starts at 0)
2.4055.5208.654
r →

The rim condition J_m(ka) = 0 says ka must be a zero of J_m. Writing j_{m,n} for the n-th positive zero, k = j_{m,n}/a and f = ck/2\pi, so 
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a}.
 Listed in order, the frequencies relative to the lowest are 1,\ 1.593,\ 2.136,\ 2.295,\ 2.653,\ 2.917, \dots No base frequency in the pitch range puts them near whole-number multiples: the zeros of each J_m are spaced by about \pi but shifted, by an amount that depends on m, and the zeros of J_0, of J_1, of J_2 and so on interleave at unrelated places. So the sound does not repeat and there is no clear pitch. Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to two modes, the cosine and the sine, which are the same pattern turned: the round head’s symmetry, visible as a multiplicity of 2.
The sand demo shows these shapes directly. The mode J_m(kr)\cos m\theta is zero where \cos m\theta = 0, at 2m angles, which pair up into m lines through the center, and along the circles where J_m(kr) = 0 inside the rim, n - 1 of them for the n-th zero. Those are exactly the lines where the sand collects.



Step-by-step derivationSeparation of variables in polar coordinates uses multivariable calculus


Look for a fixed shape. A mode is u = X(r, \theta)\cos\omega t with -\Delta X = k^2X, k = \omega/c, and X = 0 at r = a.
Laplacian in polar coordinates. \Delta X = X_{rr} + \frac1r X_r + \frac{1}{r^2}X_{\theta\theta}.
Separate. Try X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta), a separation of variables. Substituting and multiplying by r^2/(R\Theta) gives 
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta}.
 The left side depends only on r, the right only on \theta, so both equal one constant.
The angle. Going once around the drum must return \Theta to itself, so -\Theta'' = m^2\Theta with \Theta periodic. This is exactly the eigenvalue problem of the circle page: m is a whole number and \Theta = \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta.
The radius. What remains is Bessel’s equation, r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0. It has two independent solutions; one, J_m(kr), is finite at the center, and the other becomes infinite there. For m = 0 that would correspond to a point force pushing on the center of the head, and for m \ge 1 to something even more singular; in every case its energy is infinite, so it is not a free mode.
The rim. R(a) = 0 means J_m(ka) = 0, so ka must be one of the zeros j_{m,1} < j_{m,2} < \cdots of J_m.

Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero; this was conjectured by Bourget and proved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in 1929. The zeros have no closed form; this page computes them numerically. For large n they approach j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi, evenly spaced for one fixed m, but the different m interleave, and the low ones are not close to any common grid.


Where you strike. Number the modes X_1, X_2, \dots in order of frequency. A sharp strike, a brief push at a point p, gives mode i a starting speed in proportion to X_i(p), the mode’s height at the point struck, the same rule as the piano’s hammer on page 7. We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point q, which picks up mode i in proportion to X_i(q). Dividing by \iint X_i^2\,dA, the integral of the mode’s square over the head, removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode i sounds with weight X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA. (A real drum radiates sound from its whole head, and some modes radiate better than others; this model ignores that.) Strike the center and only the round modes, m = 0, sound, because every other mode has zero height there. Timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out from the center, near the still lines of several modes, which keeps those modes quiet (HyperPhysics); for the first four modes with one still circle inside, for example, that circle lies between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius. The lowest mode, which dies away fast and is not musically useful, is excited less there than by a strike at the center. Tap a stem to see one mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.

title: 8 · The drum
text:
What we found
On a surface the operator is the Laplacian. For a round drum its eigenfunctions are built from Bessel functions, and the frequencies are set by their zeros, which are not near whole-number multiples of any one frequency. That is why a drum has no clear pitch. The lines where each mode stays still are what Chladni’s sand made visible, on plates.

Pick a sound, then slide the interval between two notes of that sound and listen. The curve shows how rough each interval is.
With the string-like sound, the curve dips at 6/5, 5/4, 4/3, 3/2, 5/3 and 2: the intervals of Western harmony. Switch to the metal bar and the dips move. The octave 2 : 1 is no longer a dip; a slightly narrower interval, about 1.96, is smoother.

title: 10 · Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
Where roughness comes from
Two pure tones close in frequency produce beats: their sum swells and fades at the difference of their frequencies. Slow beats sound like a wobble, faster ones like roughness, and once the tones are far enough apart the roughness fades away. In 1965 Reinier Plomp and Willem Levelt asked listeners how dissonant pairs of pure tones sounded, as a function of their separation, and Sethares fitted a formula to their curve, written \delta below. In that formula the roughness of two pure tones near middle C is greatest when they are about 22 Hz apart, and falls off on both sides: tones much closer beat too slowly to sound rough, and tones much further apart are heard as two separate, smooth tones.
A note from a real instrument is several pure tones at once, its partials. For two such notes, Sethares adds up the roughness of every pair of partials, from either note, each weighted by the product of the two partials’ amplitudes: 
D(\alpha) = \sum_{\text{pairs } i < j} a_i a_j\; \delta\big(\min(f_i, f_j),\ |f_i - f_j|\big).
 Here the list f_1, f_2, \dots holds the partials of both notes: those of the lower note, and those of the upper note, whose frequencies are \alpha times the lower note’s; a_i is the amplitude of partial f_i. The roughness \delta of two pure tones depends on how far apart they are and, a little, on how high they are, hence its two inputs. The curve in the demo is D(\alpha).



FormulaThe roughness of two pure tones

Sethares’ fit to Plomp and Levelt’s data, for two pure tones of equal loudness, the lower at frequency f and the other x hertz above it, is 
\delta(f, x) = e^{-3.5\,s\,x} - e^{-5.75\,s\,x}, \qquad s = \frac{0.24}{0.021\,f + 19},
 with frequencies in hertz. It is zero at x = 0, rises to a peak at x = \ln(5.75/3.5)/(2.25\,s), about 22 Hz near middle C, and then decays. For tones of amplitudes a_1 and a_2, Sethares multiplies by a_1 a_2, as in D(\alpha) above. The factor s makes the roughest separation grow with the frequency, as Plomp and Levelt found: tones high up must be further apart, in hertz, to sound equally smooth. The formula describes average listeners’ judgments of roughness for pure tones; it is a fitted curve, not derived from first principles.

title: 10 · Did instruments shape our scales?
section: Why the dips sit where they do
text:
Why the dips sit where they do
For a harmonic sound, the partials of the lower note are at f, 2f, 3f, \dots and those of the upper note at \alpha f, 2\alpha f, 3\alpha f, \dots. When \alpha is a ratio of small whole numbers, say 3/2, many partials of the two notes land exactly on each other: the lower note’s third partial and the upper note’s second are both at 3f. Partials that coincide do not beat. Move \alpha off 3/2 and the pairs that coincided pull apart, by a few hertz and then by tens of hertz, into the range where beating sounds roughest. So each simple ratio sits at the bottom of a dip. The smooth intervals of a harmonic sound are the simple whole-number ratios, which extends the second idea of this series: frequencies at whole-number multiples of one frequency give a clear pitch, and they also make whole-number intervals smooth.
A uniform bar free at both ends, such as a glockenspiel bar, has the kalimba’s operator with different ends, and its partials are at 1,\ 2.756,\ 5.404,\ 8.933 times the lowest, as the fold below shows. (Xylophone and marimba bars are thinned underneath, in the middle, to move the first overtone onto a whole-number multiple, 3 on a xylophone and 4 on a marimba; gamelan bars are shaped too, as discussed below.) Now the coincidences happen elsewhere. At \alpha = 2.756 the upper note’s fundamental lands on the lower note’s second partial. At \alpha = 5.404/2.756 \approx 1.961 the upper note’s second partial lands on the lower note’s third, and that is the dip just below the octave. At \alpha = 2 nothing lines up.



Step-by-step derivationThe modes of a bar free at both ends uses a 2×2 determinant and hyperbolic functions

The operator is the bar’s \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4 from the kalimba page. A free end carries no bending moment and no shear force, so at both x = 0 and x = L the conditions are X'' = 0 and X''' = 0.

As on the kalimba page, write X = A_1\cos\beta x + A_2\sin\beta x + A_3\cosh\beta x + A_4\sinh\beta x.
At x = 0: X''(0) = \beta^2(-A_1 + A_3) = 0 and X'''(0) = \beta^3(-A_2 + A_4) = 0, so A_3 = A_1 and A_4 = A_2. Then X = A_1(\cos\beta x + \cosh\beta x) + A_2(\sin\beta x + \sinh\beta x).
At x = L, dividing by \beta^2 and \beta^3 and writing C_1 = \cos\beta L, S_1 = \sin\beta L, C_2 = \cosh\beta L, S_2 = \sinh\beta L, as on the kalimba page: 
(C_2 - C_1)\,A_1 + (S_2 - S_1)\,A_2 = 0, \qquad (S_2 + S_1)\,A_1 + (C_2 - C_1)\,A_2 = 0 .

These have a solution other than A_1 = A_2 = 0 exactly when the determinant is zero: (C_2 - C_1)^2 - (S_2 - S_1)(S_2 + S_1) = (C_2^2 - S_2^2) + (C_1^2 + S_1^2) - 2C_1C_2 = 2 - 2C_1C_2, using C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 1 and C_1^2 + S_1^2 = 1. So 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1 .
 Besides \beta = 0, which belongs to the bar moving or rotating rigidly without bending, the roots are \beta L = 4.7300,\ 7.8532,\ 10.9956,\ 14.1372, \dots, computed on this page. Since the frequency is proportional to \beta^2, the partials are at (\beta_n/\beta_1)^2 = 1,\ 2.756,\ 5.404,\ 8.933 times the lowest.

title: 10 · Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
The gamelan
Sethares measured the spectra of gamelan metallophones and reports that “the dissonance curve for these metallophones have minima that occur at or near the scale steps used by the gamelans”. The bars in the demo above are idealized uniform bars, not measured gamelan instruments, so the demo shows the mechanism, not his gamelan result; real gamelan bars are shaped and tuned by their makers, and tunings vary from one gamelan to another.

title: 10 · Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
How far does this go?
The curve measures sensory roughness, which is one ingredient of what sounds pleasant, not all of it. In a study of more than 250 American college students, Josh McDermott, Andriana Lehr and Andrew Oxenham found in 2010 that liking for consonant chords followed harmonicity, whether the frequencies fit one harmonic series (whole-number multiples f, 2f, 3f, \dots of one frequency), more than it followed beating, and grew with musical training. In 2016 McDermott and colleagues found that the Tsimane’, a society in the Bolivian Amazon with little exposure to Western music, rated consonant and dissonant chords as equally pleasant, although they disliked roughness just as other groups did.
So the spectrum decides what sounds rough, a fact about sound and the ear. What a culture finds beautiful is also learned. Sethares argues that instruments and the scales played on them tend to fit each other in the way the demo shows; how much that shaped the world’s music is an open, argued question.

title: 10 · Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
What we found
An instrument’s spectrum does not only decide whether it has a pitch. It decides which pairs of notes sound smooth together on it: for harmonic instruments, the simple whole-number ratios of Western harmony; for metal bars, other intervals. The operator of page 6, with different ends, may reach as far as the tuning of an orchestra.

title: 6b · The harmonica
text:
The reed is a valve
The operator. A reed is riveted at one end and free at the other, so everything derived on the kalimba page applies unchanged: 
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, \qquad u = u_x = 0 \text{ at the rivet}, \qquad u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \text{ at the tip}.
 The mode frequencies are in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55. For a rectangular reed of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12 and the cross-section area is S = wh, so \kappa^2 = EI/(\rho S) = Eh^2/(12\rho). With \beta_1 = 1.8751/L and \omega = \kappa\beta^2 from the kalimba page, the lowest frequency f_1 = \omega_1/2\pi is 
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
 Low reeds are long, high reeds are short. The width cancels, so it affects how much air the reed moves, not its pitch.
Plucked versus blown. Pluck a reed and it rings like a kalimba tine: you hear its own modes at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the fundamental, with the overtones dying almost at once. Blow it and the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path. The sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow; Pykett notes that very little sound comes from the reed’s own motion. A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats itself exactly, at a playing frequency f_p slightly below its first mode’s frequency f_1, so the pattern of airflow repeats at that rate too. Why does it lock? A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, while the reed’s other modes are not sustained at their own frequencies, so the motion settles into one repeating cycle; in that cycle the other modes move only as they are driven, at whole-number multiples of f_p. A periodic signal has partials only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate, so the blown note is harmonic, with strong odd and even partials (Pykett), even though the reed’s own overtones are not. The harmonics come from the valve action, the slot being open for only part of each cycle, not from the reed’s modes.



Why it worksA steady puff train has whole-number partials uses Fourier series (page 3)

Let q(t) be the airflow through the slot. Once the blown reed has settled into its steady oscillation, the opening, and so q, repeats every P = 1/f_p seconds: q(t + P) = q(t). A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push, like this one, is called a self-sustained oscillation, and the repeating cycle it settles into a limit cycle; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others. That it settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. By the circle page, a periodic function of period P is a Fourier series in \cos(2\pi nt/P) and \sin(2\pi nt/P), so it contains only the frequencies n f_p. How strong each one is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials. The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up, which is why the reed’s own overtone frequencies, 6.27 and 17.55 times f_1, do not appear.
The demo’s sound is a model: one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency, then passed through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player’s mouth and the instrument. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.


The same mechanism drives the bowed string and the clarinet: a steady push, from the bow or the breath, turned into a periodic oscillation. On those instruments the operator’s own frequencies are already nearly whole-number multiples, so the excitation and the operator agree, and locking is easy. A free reed’s are not, which lets you hear that the excitation, not the operator, sets the overtones.
Tuning a reed with a file. Reed makers tune by scraping metal off, and where they scrape decides the direction. The Rayleigh quotient explains why. For the first mode, 
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
 the minimum taken over shapes, not identically zero, that satisfy the conditions at the rivet; the minimizing shape is the first mode itself. This is \omega^2 = k/m from page 1 again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. The first mode is the shape that makes this ratio as small as possible. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thinning the reed near the rivet removes stiffness where it counts and lowers the pitch; thinning it near the tip removes mass where it counts and raises it.


    Where to filebase
    
    Blow the filed reedBlow the original
    Filing removes 25% of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change uses the unfiled mode shape in the Rayleigh quotient, which is accurate when the filing is shallow.
  




Step-by-step derivationThe effect of a little filing uses integration by parts and a first-order approximation


The quotient. Multiply \rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')'' by X and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip, as on the kalimba page. This gives \omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2 for every mode.
Small change. File the reed so that its thickness changes by \delta h(x) < 0. Then I \propto h^3 changes by \delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h, and S \propto h changes by \delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h, to first order, that is, ignoring terms in (\delta h)^2.
First order. Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape X and change only the coefficients: 
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,\big(3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2\big)\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}.

Sign. Near the rivet X \approx 0 and X'' is largest, so the bracket is positive and, with \delta h < 0, \omega drops. Near the tip X'' = 0 and X is largest, so the bracket is negative and \omega rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.


The chromatic slide. A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reed chambers, the second tuned a semitone higher. Each hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a draw reed, sounded by breathing in, in each set. Pushing the slide moves a perforated bar that closes one set and opens the other, so every note rises a semitone. In solo tuning, the usual layout for a chromatic harmonica, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw.

title: 6b · The harmonica
text:
What we found
The operator decides which frequencies an object can vibrate at; the way it is driven decides what you hear. A harmonica reed has the kalimba’s operator and its scattered overtones, but blowing makes it a valve that chops the air into a regular train of puffs, and a regular train has exactly whole-number partials.

Start with the simplest thing that vibrates: a mass on a spring. Pull it down and let go, and it bobs at a steady rate, faster with a stiffer spring and slower with a heavier mass. Now change how far you pull it. It travels further, but each bob takes exactly as long.

title: 1 · One mass on a spring
section: Why the size of the swing doesn’t matter
text:
Why the size of the swing doesn’t matter
A spring pulled a distance x from its resting position (for a hanging spring, the position where the spring’s pull balances gravity) pulls back with force -kx: this is Hooke’s law, and the constant k is the spring’s stiffness. Newton’s second law says force equals mass times acceleration, so 
m\,\ddot x = -k\,x, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \ddot x = -\lambda\,x \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda = k/m .
 Here \ddot x means the second derivative of position with respect to time, the acceleration. Try a steady oscillation x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi). Differentiating twice gives \ddot x = -\omega^2 x, so it solves the equation exactly when \omega^2 = \lambda. The number \omega is the angular frequency, in radians per second. The cosine repeats each time \omega t grows by 2\pi, so one cycle takes 2\pi/\omega seconds, and the motion repeats f = \omega/2\pi times a second: 
f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} .
 The amplitude A and the starting phase \phi are free: they record how you started the motion, and they do not appear in f. A real string also loses energy, which this model leaves out. Adding a friction force proportional to the velocity, -2m\gamma\,\dot x, gives x = Ae^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t + \phi) with \omega_d = \sqrt{k/m - \gamma^2}, as long as the friction is light (\gamma^2 < k/m); differentiating twice checks it. The swing shrinks, so the motion no longer repeats exactly, but the rate of its swings, \omega_d, still does not depend on A.



ProofEvery motion is of this form, and the pitch cannot depend on amplitude uses the uniqueness of solutions of a differential equation

Every solution is A\cos(\omega t + \phi). The equation \ddot x = -\lambda x is linear: sums and multiples of solutions are solutions. A solution is determined by its starting position x(0) and starting velocity \dot x(0); this is the uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations. The functions \cos\omega t and \sin\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt\lambda, are solutions with starting data (1, 0) and (0, \omega). So the solution with data (x_0, v_0) is x_0\cos\omega t + (v_0/\omega)\sin\omega t. By the formula \cos(\omega t + \phi) = \cos\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\sin\phi, this equals A\cos(\omega t + \phi) with A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + (v_0/\omega)^2}, \cos\phi = x_0/A and \sin\phi = -v_0/(\omega A).
Amplitude cannot change the pitch. If x(t) is a solution, so is 2x(t), by linearity, and it has the same period. Real springs stop obeying Hooke’s law when stretched far; then the equation is no longer linear and the frequency does depend on amplitude (anharmonicity). Strings show a small version of this: a hard pluck stretches the string, raising its tension, so the note starts slightly sharp and settles as it fades. For the gentle vibrations of most playing, the linear law holds well.

title: 1 · One mass on a spring
section: The operator, in its smallest form
text:
The operator, in its smallest form
Write the equation as \ddot x = -\lambda x. The restoring force per unit mass is -\lambda x: multiply the displacement by \lambda and reverse its direction. We call the rule “multiply by \lambda” the operator, and keep the minus sign in the equation. The one allowed angular frequency is \omega = \sqrt\lambda.
On the next page the single displacement x becomes a list of displacements, one per bead, and the number \lambda becomes a table of numbers, a matrix. Later it becomes a rule acting on whole shapes, a differential operator. The pattern never changes: the allowed angular frequencies \omega = 2\pi f are the square roots of the operator’s eigenvalues, the numbers by which it rescales its special shapes. The next page defines them properly; for one mass there is one eigenvalue, the number \lambda = k/m itself.

title: 1 · One mass on a spring
text:
What we found
Newton’s law, with a restoring force proportional to the displacement, allows exactly one frequency. It is set by the stiffness and the mass, not by how far the mass swings, and that is why a fading note keeps its pitch, to a very good approximation.
