Listen to an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1, then to a stretched one. The slow wobble in loudness is called a beat.
Then play the whole piano with the mouse or your computer keys. Release a key and its felt damper drops back onto the string and stops it.

title: 7 · The piano
text:
Two restoring forces at once
The operator. Forces per unit length add. Tension contributes T\,u_{xx}, as for the string, and bending contributes -EI\,u_{xxxx}, as for the kalimba, so with \mu the mass per unit length (density times cross-section area, the \rho S of the kalimba page) 
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \quad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 ,
 with c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu. Here \partial_x^2 means two derivatives in x, the same as the subscript xx, and \mathcal{L} is this page’s operator, playing the role A played before. Treat the ends as pinned: held in place but free to pivot, so u = 0 and, since a pivot exerts no bending moment and the moment is EI\,u_{xx}, also u_{xx} = 0. Real piano strings are held a little more firmly than that, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.



Step-by-step derivationFrom Newton’s law on a short piece of wire to the operator and its spectrum uses partial derivatives

1. One small piece. Follow the stretch of wire between x and x+dx. Its mass is \mu\,dx and its vertical acceleration is u_{tt}, so Newton’s law says \mu\,dx\,u_{tt} equals the net vertical force on it. Two forces act: the pull of tension, and the wire’s resistance to bending.
2. Tension. The rest of the string pulls on each end of the piece with force T, along the string.

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx+dx
  T uₓ(x)curved piece, mass μ dx
  T uₓ(x+dx)

At the right end the pull points along the slope u_x(x+dx), so for small slopes its vertical part is T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T\,u_x(x+dx). At the left end it is -T\,u_x(x). Together they give T\,[u_x(x+dx) - u_x(x)] \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx. A curved piece feels a net pull toward its center of curvature; a straight piece feels none.
3. Bending. The wire also resists bending, exactly like the kalimba’s tine. The kalimba page derives the bending force per unit length, -EI\,u_{xxxx}, where E is steel’s Young’s modulus and I = \pi d^4/64 is the second moment of area of a round wire of diameter d.
4. Newton’s law. Adding the two forces gives \mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx - EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx. Dividing by \mu\,dx, with c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, 
u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 .

5. Ends. The bridge at one end and a metal bearing point at the other hold the wire in place, so u = 0. If they let the wire pivot freely, they exert no moment, so M = EI\,u_{xx} = 0. These are the pinned conditions u = u_{xx} = 0.
6. Spectrum. Try u = \sin(kx)\cos(\omega t) with k = n\pi/L, which satisfies both pinned conditions. Then u_{xx} = -k^2u and u_{xxxx} = k^4u, so the equation becomes -\omega^2 = -c^2k^2 - \kappa^2k^4, that is 
\omega^2 = c^2k^2\Big(1 + \frac{EI}{T}\,k^2\Big) = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2\Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}\,n^2\Big).
 Taking square roots gives f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, with f_0 = c/2L and B = \pi^2EI/TL^2.
7. How big is B? For a middle C wire, roughly d = 1 mm and L = 0.6 m, with steel’s E = 2\times10^{11} Pa and density 7850 kg/m³; a tension of about 610 N then gives middle C. So I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14} m^4 and B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}. The 10th partial, at 10f_0\sqrt{1 + 100B}, then sits 1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental f_0\sqrt{1 + B}. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.
8. What was assumed. Small slopes; tension unchanged as the wire flexes; the wire’s rotational inertia neglected (Rayleigh’s correction adds a small term); a uniform wire.


Spectrum. Pinned ends make \sin(n\pi x/L) an eigenfunction of both terms at once, so here the two operators’ eigenvalues simply add; that is special to pinned ends, where the two operators share their eigenfunctions, and with clamped ends the formula needs a small correction. Substituting gives \omega^2 = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2 k^4 with k = n\pi/L, so 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{T L^2},
 where f_0 = c/2L is the lowest frequency the same string would have without stiffness. The actual fundamental is f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}.
The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so high partials run noticeably sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic. For a middle C wire B is about 4.4\times10^{-4}, and the 10th partial sits about 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental; the fold above has the arithmetic. Since I grows like the fourth power of the wire’s diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.

title: 7 · The piano
text:
Why exact octaves beat
A tuner sets an octave by listening for beats, a slow wobble in loudness, between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Beats happen when two nearly equal frequencies add, at a rate equal to their difference. The lower note’s fundamental is f_0\sqrt{1+B} and its second partial is 2f_0\sqrt{1+4B}. Their ratio is 2\sqrt{(1+4B)/(1+B)} \approx 2\,(1 + 2B)(1 - B/2) \approx 2\,(1 + 3B/2), using \sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 + x/2 and 1/\sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 - x/2 for small x: the second partial is more than twice the fundamental by a factor of about 1 + 3B/2. An upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental therefore sits a little below that second partial, and the two beat. To silence the beats the tuner raises the upper note until its fundamental matches the lower note’s second partial, which makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of them at once, so real tuning is a compromise. Repeated across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: compared with equal temperament, in which every semitone is exactly the ratio 2^{1/12}, the top of a piano is tuned sharp and the bottom flat.
That answers the opening puzzle: on a stiff string, “exactly 2 : 1” lines up the wrong pair of frequencies.

title: 7 · The piano
text:
Hammer, dampers and pedals
A second question: what do the pedals actually do to the sound? None of them moves a frequency, apart from tiny shifts explained below.
The operator is only part of the string’s equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy to damping; here f(x,t) is a force, not a frequency: 
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).

Each term has one job. The operator, T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing f is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping b is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches acts on f or on b. Only the tuner’s wrench, which changes T, touches the operator.
Both effects are read off the mode shapes X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L). A hammer blow at x_h gives mode n a weight proportional to X_n(x_h), the mode’s own height at the hammer. The drum on the next page uses the same rule. A damper felt resting on a short stretch W of the string makes mode n’s swing shrink like e^{-\gamma_n t}, and for weak damping (to first order in b, that is, ignoring terms in b^2) the decay rate is 
\gamma_n = \frac{\int_W b\,X_n^2\,dx}{2\mu\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx}.
 A mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and its frequency shifts only by an amount proportional to \gamma_n^2, negligible for weak damping. A mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper: in the view below, slide the damper to L/8, where the hammer also sits, and the 8th mode, which has a still point there, is not excited and barely damped.



Step-by-step derivationWhere the hammer weights and the damping rates come from uses integrals of products of modes and a first-order approximation

1. Expand in modes. Write u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x), with \mathcal{L}X_n = \omega_n^2X_n and the pinned conditions.
2. Project. Substitute into the full equation, multiply by X_m and integrate along the string. The operator is symmetric with these boundary conditions (in fact self-adjoint), by integrating by parts as on the circle page, so the X_n are orthogonal: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each: 
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n D_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
 with N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx, D_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx and F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx.
3. The hammer. The felt touches a short stretch near x_h, so F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t), where P(t) is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by X_m(x_h): the mode’s own height at the hammer.
4. The damper. If the damping is weak, the cross terms D_{mn} with m \ne n change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode, 
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{D_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
 whose solution e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big) decays at the rate \gamma_m while its frequency moves only by order \gamma_m^2/\omega_m.
5. Honest limits. A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

On a grand piano the middle pedal is usually the sostenuto, which holds up only the dampers of keys already down. Most notes have two or three strings, and Weinreich showed that their coupling through the bridge, each string’s motion slightly shaking the others, produces the piano’s two-stage decay: a loud start that fades fast, then a quiet, long aftersound. A grand’s soft pedal strikes fewer of the strings, so the coupled motion starts differently. This model leaves the coupling out.

Where the dampers touch the string matters, and the formula for \gamma_n says why. Mode n is damped in proportion to its motion under the felt. Close to an end every low mode barely moves, so a damper there hardly damps the bass. In most modern uprights the dampers sit below the hammers, nearer the middle of the string; in older “birdcage” uprights they sat above the hammers, near the end. Piano restorers report that the under-damper design stops the strings better, partly because its dampers are closer to the middle of the string (Sykes). The slider in the view above moves the damper and shows the effect on each mode.



Reader questionWhat does a damper do, and what would a piano without dampers sound like?

Without dampers, releasing a key would do nothing: every string would ring until it died on its own, exactly as if the sustain pedal were always down. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.

title: 7 · The piano
text:
What we found
Operators add. A piano wire is pulled tight like a string and resists bending like a bar, so its operator is the sum of the two, and its overtones run slightly sharp of the whole numbers. The rest of a real string’s equation, damping and forcing, is where the hammer, the dampers and the pedals act, and none of them moves a frequency, apart from tiny shifts that weak damping causes.

Here are six sounds that need explaining. Play them, and try to guess why each one happens.
And one question beyond the mathematics: did the instruments people built shape the scales they play? That is the epilogue.

title: Instruments as Operators
text:
Two ideas answer all six

An instrument’s frequencies come from the spectrum of an operator. The operator is a rule that takes a shape of the instrument, a bent string or a dented drumhead, and gives back the force pulling it back toward rest (per unit mass, and with a minus sign, so that the motion obeys u_{tt} = -Au, where u is the shape, u_{tt} its acceleration and A the operator). The shapes it only rescales are the instrument’s modes; the rescaling factors are its eigenvalues, and the list of them is the spectrum. Each frequency is proportional to the square root of an eigenvalue. The simplest case is a loop of string, where the operator is -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2, minus the second derivative times a constant c^2, and writing a shape in its modes is the Fourier series.
A clear pitch means the frequencies you hear sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency, a frequency in the range we hear as pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand hertz. Then the sound repeats, or nearly repeats, and the repetition rate is the pitch. Since the frequencies come from the spectrum, whether they line up is decided by the operator and the instrument’s shape. How you play decides how loud each frequency is, with one refinement: a steady bow or breath can lock the motion into exact repetition, close to one of the operator’s frequencies, even when the operator’s overtones are off the grid.

title: Instruments as Operators
text:
Families


Instruments that are the same up to constants

Instruments in one family share one rule for the restoring force, so they are close to the same mathematical object with different constants. title: 5 · An air column
text:
Same equation, other ends
The operator. Let p(x, t) be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure. It obeys the wave equation again, 
p_{tt} = c^2 p_{xx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} \approx (343\ \text{m/s})^2,
 where \rho is the density of air and K its bulk modulus, its resistance to being squeezed (this K has nothing to do with the bead matrix of page 2). The constant c is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C. So the operator is again -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, now acting on pressure shapes along the tube.



Step-by-step derivationNewton’s law for a slab of air uses partial derivatives


  
  
  
  
  p(x)p(x+dx)
  slab, mass ρS dx


Let \xi(x, t) be how far the air that normally sits at x has moved along the tube, and let the tube’s cross-section have area S.
The slab of air between x and x + dx has mass \rho S\,dx. The only force on it along the tube is the pressure difference between its two faces, S\,[p(x) - p(x + dx)] \approx -S\,p_x\,dx. Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, divided by S\,dx, is \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x.
The slab’s two faces move by \xi(x) and \xi(x + dx), so its length changes by \xi(x + dx) - \xi(x) \approx \xi_x\,dx: it is stretched by the fraction \xi_x, and its pressure drops in proportion: p = -K\,\xi_x. In a sound wave the squeezing is too fast for heat to flow, which is called adiabatic; for air this makes K about 1.4 times atmospheric pressure.
Differentiate step 2 in x and step 3 twice in t: \rho\,\xi_{ttx} = -p_{xx} and p_{tt} = -K\,\xi_{xtt}. Eliminating \xi gives p_{tt} = (K/\rho)\,p_{xx}.

What was assumed: the tube is narrow compared with the sound’s wavelength, so the pressure is the same across it, and the pressure changes are small. Friction with the walls is left out.


Boundary conditions. At an open end the air in the tube meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure: p = 0. This is approximate: the air just outside moves with the air inside, so the tube acts as if it were slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius at each open end, an amount called the end correction. At the clarinet’s reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth. Air that never moves has no acceleration, so the net push on it is zero; that push is set by how fast the pressure changes along the tube, p_x, so p_x = 0 there (step 2 of the derivation, with \xi the air’s displacement along the tube). The first of these is the string’s Dirichlet condition. The second, a condition on the slope, is called a Neumann condition.
Spectrum. A mode is a pressure shape X(x) with -X'' = k^2 X, so X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, and its frequency is f = ck/2\pi. For the clarinet, X'(0) = bk = 0 at the reed forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 at the open end needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2 and f_n = (2n-1)c/4L. For the flute, open at both ends, the conditions are the string’s, and give \sin(n\pi x/L). So

Two consequences can be heard in the demo.

An octave lower, almost. An octave is a frequency ratio of 2. The same ideal tube sounds c/4L closed at one end but c/2L open at both, exactly an octave lower. Real flutes and clarinets differ a little in length, the clarinet’s mouthpiece and bell change its effective length, and the end corrections differ, so the real interval comes out a bit less than an octave.
A twelfth, not an octave. The clarinet’s register key opens a small hole near the top of the tube. An open hole lets air in and out, pulling the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the lower part of the low register (the notes played without the key), the hole sits about a third of the way down the sounding tube, right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode (Wolfe). For the other notes the hole is off that point, well off for the lowest and highest notes you play with the key (Wolfe), and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, and the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency it moves more easily, so the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the higher frequency of the 3f_1 mode it moves much less, so the hole acts almost as a plug. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode. That is a ratio of 3, called a twelfth: an octave and a fifth, where a fifth is the ratio 3/2. A flutist overblows without a key, by blowing faster, and the flute’s next mode is 2f_1, an octave. That is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart and flute fingerings an octave apart.




ProofWhy only odd harmonics: the closed tube is a quarter of a loop uses the circle’s eigenfunctions (page 3)

Use the reflections from the string page. Take a pressure shape p on [0, L] with p_x(0) = 0 and p(L) = 0.

Reflect it evenly across the reed end, p(-x) = p(x). A smooth even shape has zero slope at 0, so even reflection is what the Neumann condition p_x(0) = 0 allows, so the result is a shape on [-L, L] that vanishes at both ends.
Reflect that oddly across x = L, p(2L - x) = -p(x), and repeat. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 4L.
On that loop the eigenfunctions are \cos(k\pi x/2L) and \sin(k\pi x/2L). Step 1 keeps only cosines. Step 2 needs \cos\big(k\pi(2L - x)/2L\big) = (-1)^k\cos(k\pi x/2L) to equal -\cos(k\pi x/2L), which keeps only odd k.

So the clarinet’s modes are the odd harmonics of a loop four tube-lengths long, which is where both the factor 4 and the odd numbers come from.


The reed. The reed is a valve. When the pressure in the mouthpiece drops, it closes, and when the pressure rises, it opens, so the air column, through the pressure it creates, drives the reed that feeds it. In normal playing this settles into a periodic oscillation, like the bowed string, at a playing frequency close to the tube’s lowest mode. A periodic sound can have partials only at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, but it may have them at all of them, so the distinction matters: the tube’s modes are odd multiples only, but the clarinet’s sound contains even harmonics too. In the low register, the lowest notes of the instrument, the even harmonics are weak because the tube has no resonance to support them, but they are not absent. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine these numbers, not the picture.

title: 5 · An air column
text:
What we found
The string’s operator also governs the air pressure in a tube. Changing the boundary condition at one end, from “pressure equals the room’s” to “the air cannot move”, halves the lowest frequency and keeps only its odd multiples: the clarinet’s modes are at 1, 3, 5, … times c/4L. In the sound, which repeats, the even harmonics are weak rather than gone.

title: 5 · An air column
text:
The next puzzle
So far every restoring force has been a pull or a push along the material: tension along a string, pressure along a tube. A kalimba tine is different, because nothing stretches it. Halve a string’s length and its pitch rises one octave; halve a tine’s length and its pitch rises two. Why?

title: Glossary
text:
Sound

Hertz (Hz)

One cycle per second, the unit of frequency. The A above middle C is tuned to 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Periodic

A signal p(t) is periodic with period P > 0 if it repeats exactly every P seconds: p(t + P) = p(t) for all t. Its shortest such P is usually what is meant by the period. Wikipedia

Pitch

How high or low a note sounds. For a periodic sound with shortest period P, the pitch is heard at the repetition rate 1/P, even when no component at that frequency is present, as long as that rate is between a few dozen and a few thousand per second. Wikipedia, and page 0

Partial, overtone

A sound can be split into components of single frequencies; each one is a partial. An overtone is any partial above the lowest. Wikipedia

Fundamental

For a periodic sound, the frequency f = 1/P at which it repeats; its harmonics are the whole-number multiples of f. It is usually the lowest and strongest partial, but it can be weak or even missing, and the pitch is still heard at f (page 0). For a sound that is not periodic, such as a drum’s, “fundamental” just means the lowest partial. Wikipedia

Harmonic

A partial at a whole-number multiple nf of the fundamental. A periodic sound contains only harmonics. Wikipedia

Harmonic series

The whole-number multiples f, 2f, 3f, \dots of one frequency f. All the partials of a periodic sound belong to one harmonic series. Wikipedia

Inharmonic

Having partials that are not whole-number multiples of one frequency. A bell, a drum and a kalimba tine are strongly inharmonic; a piano string is slightly inharmonic. Wikipedia

Timbre

What tells two notes of the same pitch and loudness apart, such as a violin and a flute both playing A. It depends mostly on the relative strengths of the partials and how they change over the course of the note. Wikipedia

Note names: C4, A4, middle C

Notes are named by a letter from A to G and an octave number. C4 is middle C, about 262 Hz, near the middle of the piano keyboard; C5 is the C an octave above it; A4 is the A at 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Semitone

The smallest step on a piano, from one key to the next, white or black. Twelve semitones make an octave. Wikipedia

Equal temperament

The usual way of tuning a piano: every semitone is the same frequency ratio, 2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595, so twelve of them make an exact octave. The price is that the other intervals miss the simple ratios slightly: an equal-tempered fifth is 2^{7/12} \approx 1.4983, not 3/2. Wikipedia

Cent

A unit for small differences in pitch: one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone, so an octave is 1200 cents. Two frequencies in the ratio r are 1200\log_2 r cents apart. Trained listeners notice a few cents. Wikipedia

Octave, fifth, twelfth

Musical intervals, named by frequency ratio. An octave is a ratio of 2. A fifth is the ratio 3/2 when tuned to the simple ratio, and 2^{7/12} \approx 1.498 in equal temperament. A twelfth, an octave plus a fifth, is about 3. Two notes an octave apart sound like “the same note, higher”. Wikipedia

Beats

When two pure tones of nearly equal frequency sound together, their sum swells and fades in loudness at a rate equal to the difference of their frequencies. Tuners listen for beats; fast beats are heard as roughness. Wikipedia

Consonance, roughness

Consonance is how smooth or stable two notes sound together. Roughness is one ingredient of it: the harsh quality of fast beats between partials that are close but not equal. Wikipedia, and the epilogue

title: Glossary
text:
Instrument parts and playing

Nut, bridge

On a string instrument, the two points that end a string’s vibrating length: the nut at the top of the neck, the bridge on the body. The bridge also carries the string’s vibration to the body, or on a piano to the soundboard. On a kalimba, the bridge is the bar the tines are pressed against. Wikipedia

Open string

A string played with no finger pressing it down, so its whole length between the nut and the bridge vibrates. Wikipedia

Harmonics, on a string

Notes a string player gets by touching the string lightly at a fraction of its length, such as the middle, instead of pressing it down. Only the modes with a still point under the finger keep sounding. Wikipedia, and page 4

Overblowing, register key

Making a wind instrument’s air column jump to a higher mode. A flutist overblows by blowing faster; a clarinetist presses the register key, which opens a small hole that spoils the lowest mode. Wikipedia, and page 5

Blow, draw

On a harmonica, a blow note sounds when you breathe out through a hole, and a draw note when you breathe in. Each hole has one reed for each (on a chromatic harmonica, one for each in each of its two sets). Wikipedia

Free reed

A thin metal tongue fixed at one end that swings through a closely fitting slot, opening and shutting it like a valve. Harmonicas and accordions use free reeds. Wikipedia

Damper

A felt pad that rests on a piano string and stops it when the key is released. Each key lifts its own damper while held; the right pedal lifts them all. The highest strings, roughly the top 20 keys, have no dampers. Wikipedia: Sustain pedal

Soft pedal, una corda

The left pedal of a piano. On a grand it shifts the hammers sideways so they hit fewer strings; this is the una corda, Italian for “one string”. On an upright it instead moves the hammers closer to the strings, so they strike more gently. Wikipedia

Practice pedal, mute

The middle pedal on many uprights. It lowers a strip of felt between the hammers and the strings, making the sound much quieter and duller. Wikipedia: Piano pedals

title: Glossary
text:
Vibration

Partial derivative, u_t, u_{xx}

For a function of several variables, such as the height u(x, t) of a string at position x and time t, the rate of change in one variable with the others held fixed. Subscripts name the variable: u_t is the velocity of the point at x, u_{tt} its acceleration, u_x the slope of the string, and u_{xx} how fast that slope changes along it, which for small slopes is its curvature. Wikipedia

Proportional, \propto

a \propto b means that a is a fixed number times b. So f \propto 1/L^2 means that halving L multiplies f by four. Wikipedia

Angular frequency

\omega = 2\pi f: the frequency counted in radians per second instead of cycles per second, one cycle being 2\pi radians. Formulas such as \omega^2 = k/m are shortest in \omega. Wikipedia

Wavenumber

The counterpart of angular frequency in space: a wave \sin kx has wavenumber k = 2\pi/\text{wavelength}. For the wave equation, \omega = ck. Wikipedia

Linear

An equation with no outside force is linear if sums and multiples of solutions are again solutions. An equation with an outside force is linear when it reads (left side) = (the force), where the force does not involve u, and the left side is built from u and its derivatives only by multiplying each by a number, or by a given function of position and time, and adding: no u^2, no u\,u_x, no \sin u. The piano page’s \mu u_{tt} + b\,u_t - Tu_{xx} + EI\,u_{xxxx} = f(x, t) is an example. Then the difference of any two solutions solves the same equation without the force. The operators in this series are linear, a good model for the small vibrations of instruments. What keeps a bowed string, a clarinet reed or a harmonica reed going is not linear: the bow’s grip and slip and a reed opening and closing. Wikipedia

Superposition

Adding solutions of a linear equation to get another solution. The free motion of an instrument, once nothing is driving it, is a superposition, a sum, of its modes. Wikipedia

Mode, normal mode

A motion of an object, with no friction and nothing driving it, in which every part swings at the same single frequency and the overall shape stays the same, only growing and shrinking. Every small free vibration is a sum of modes. Wikipedia

Standing wave

A wave whose shape stays in place, such as a mode of a string. It can be seen as two equal waves traveling in opposite directions. Wikipedia

Node, antinode, nodal line

A node is a point of a standing wave that does not move; an antinode is a point that moves the most. Touching a string lightly at a node of a mode does not disturb that mode. On a drumhead or a plate, a mode stays still along whole curves, its nodal lines; Chladni’s sand collects on them. Wikipedia

Wave equation

The equation u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} for the height u(x, t) of a stretched string, and its relatives for air in a pipe and for a drumhead. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels. Wikipedia, and page 3

Boundary condition

A rule for what happens at the edge of a vibrating object, set by how it is held. A string tied down at an end has u = 0 there. A bar clamped at an end can neither move nor tilt there: u = 0 and u_x = 0. At the open end of a pipe the pressure equals room pressure. Wikipedia, and page 4

Dirichlet and Neumann conditions

Two kinds of boundary condition. A Dirichlet condition fixes the value at the edge, such as u = 0 at a string’s tied end or p = 0 at a pipe’s open end. A Neumann condition fixes the slope, such as p_x = 0 at a clarinet’s reed end. Wikipedia: Dirichlet, Neumann

Damping

Friction that drains energy from a vibration, so that it dies away. A term b\,u_t in the equation, proportional to velocity, is the simplest model. Wikipedia

Self-sustained oscillation, limit cycle

An oscillation kept going at a steady size by a steady supply of energy, such as a bow drawn at constant speed or a steady breath. In normal playing the motion settles into one repeating cycle, called a limit cycle; under some conditions it does not, as in the unsteady, warbling wolf note of some cellos. This needs a mechanism that is not linear, such as the bow’s grip and slip or a reed opening and closing. Wikipedia

Coupling

Two vibrating parts are coupled when the motion of one pushes on the other, as when piano strings share a bridge. Coupled parts trade energy, and their modes mix. Wikipedia

Helmholtz motion

The way a bowed string moves. The string sticks to the bow, slips back, and sticks again; seen from the side, a single sharp corner races back and forth along the string, one round trip per period. J. Wolfe, UNSW: The bowed string

Cantilever, clamped bar

A bar fixed rigidly at one end, so that end can neither move nor tilt, and free at the other, like a diving board. A kalimba tine is close to a cantilever: it is pressed against a bridge near one end and its tip is free. Wikipedia

Euler–Bernoulli beam

The standard model of a bending bar under no tension: \mu u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}, where \mu is the mass per unit length, E the Young’s modulus and I the second moment of area. The bar resists being bent, and bending is curvature, two derivatives; balancing forces along the bar adds two more, giving four. Wikipedia

Bending moment, shear force

Imagine cutting a bent bar at some point. The bending moment is the turning effect that one side exerts on the other, which tries to bend the bar; the shear force is the sideways force across the cut. A free end carries neither. Wikipedia: Bending moment, Shear force

Young’s modulus

How stiff a material is when stretched: the force per unit area needed, divided by the fraction by which it lengthens. Steel is about 200 GPa; nylon, used for classical guitar strings, is a few GPa. Wikipedia

Second moment of area

How the shape of a bar’s cross-section resists bending, written I. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12: doubling the thickness makes the bar eight times harder to bend. Wikipedia

Hyperbolic functions, cosh and sinh

\cosh x = (e^x + e^{-x})/2 and \sinh x = (e^x - e^{-x})/2. They satisfy \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1, much as \cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1. In a bar they describe the part of the bending that grows or fades along the bar instead of wiggling. Wikipedia

Bulk modulus, adiabatic

How hard a material is to compress: the pressure needed, divided by the fraction by which the volume shrinks. In a sound wave the squeezes are too quick for heat to flow in or out, which is called adiabatic, and for air this gives about 1.4 \times atmospheric pressure. Wikipedia

First-order approximation

Keeping only the terms proportional to a small change and dropping those proportional to its square and higher powers. For a small \varepsilon, (1 + \varepsilon)^3 = 1 + 3\varepsilon + 3\varepsilon^2 + \varepsilon^3 \approx 1 + 3\varepsilon to first order. A second-order approximation keeps the \varepsilon^2 terms too. Wikipedia

title: Glossary
text:
Matrices and operators

Matrix times vector

For a square matrix K and a list of numbers v, the product Kv is the list whose j-th entry is \sum_k K_{jk}v_k: row j of K, multiplied entry by entry with v and added up. Wikipedia

Eigenvector, eigenvalue

A nonzero vector v that a matrix K only rescales, multiplying it by a number \lambda: Kv = \lambda v. The number \lambda is the eigenvalue. On the bead ring of page 2, v lists how far each bead is displaced and Kv the forces pulling them back, up to a constant; an eigenvector is a shape in which each bead is pulled back in proportion to its own displacement, so all the beads swing at one frequency. Eigenvalues are squared angular frequencies, up to a constant. Wikipedia

Eigenvalue

See eigenvector.

Multiplicity

The number of independent eigenvectors that share one eigenvalue. Vectors are independent when none of them is a combination of the others. On a ring, the cosine and sine shapes of the same wave are two independent modes with the same frequency, so that frequency has multiplicity 2. Wikipedia

Perpendicular, orthogonal

Two vectors are perpendicular, or orthogonal, when their dot product, the sum of the products of matching entries, is zero. For functions the dot product is replaced by the inner product. Wikipedia

Symmetric matrix

A square matrix of real numbers equal to its own mirror image across the diagonal: the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. The spectral theorem says its eigenvalues are real and it has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors. Wikipedia

Determinant

A number computed from a square matrix that is zero exactly when the matrix sends some nonzero vector to zero. So linear equations with all right-hand sides zero have a solution other than all zeros exactly when the determinant of their coefficients is zero. For a 2\times2 matrix with rows (p, q) and (r, s) it is ps - qr. Wikipedia

Circulant matrix

A square matrix in which each row is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around. Whatever its entries, the complex waves e^{2\pi ijk/N} of the discrete Fourier transform, the next entry, are eigenvectors of it; when the matrix is also symmetric, as on page 2, so are the real cosine and sine waves. Wikipedia

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)

Writing a list of N numbers, indexed by j = 0, \dots, N-1, as a sum of the waves \cos(2\pi jk/N) and \sin(2\pi jk/N) for k = 0, \dots, N-1; with Euler’s formula these are combined into e^{2\pi ijk/N}. Wikipedia, and page 2

Euler’s formula

e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta, where i^2 = -1. It packs a cosine and a sine into one expression that is easier to multiply and differentiate. Wikipedia

Operator

A rule that takes a function and returns another function. In this series the operator A takes a shape u of the instrument and returns minus the restoring force on it, per unit mass, so that the motion obeys u_{tt} = -Au. It comes with its allowed shapes, those that obey the boundary conditions. All of these operators are linear. Example: A = -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2 on shapes of a loop. Pages 3 and 4 drop the constant c^2 and work with -d^2/d\theta^2, whose eigenvalues \lambda give frequencies c\sqrt\lambda/2\pi. Wikipedia

Eigenfunction

A nonzero function f that an operator only rescales: Af = \lambda f. Example: -\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\cos 3\theta = 9\cos 3\theta. Wikipedia

Spectrum

For every instrument in this series, the list of its operator’s eigenvalues; the frequencies are their square roots divided by 2\pi (when the constant c^2 is dropped from the operator, multiply by c too). (In general, for an operator on an infinite-dimensional space, the spectrum is the set of numbers \lambda for which A - \lambda has no well-behaved inverse, which can contain more than eigenvalues.) Wikipedia

Inner product

A way to multiply two vectors or two functions to get a number, generalizing the dot product. For functions on the circle, \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta, where \bar g is the complex conjugate of g, which is just g when g is real. Two functions are perpendicular if it is zero. Wikipedia

L^2(S^1)

The space of functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite, with the inner product above. (For readers who know measure theory: two functions that differ only on a set of measure zero count as the same.) It is where the shapes of a vibrating loop live. Wikipedia

Symmetric and self-adjoint operators

An operator A is symmetric if \langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle for all allowed f and g, the analogue of a symmetric matrix. That alone makes its eigenvalues real and its eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues perpendicular. Self-adjoint is a stronger condition on the set of allowed shapes, roughly that it is neither too small nor too large. Together with a further property that every instrument here has, it is what the spectral theorem needs to give enough eigenfunctions to build every shape (page 3). (For readers who know functional analysis: self-adjoint means A = A^*, domains included; for the loop the domain is H^2(S^1), and the further property is that (A + 1)^{-1} is compact.) Wikipedia

Fourier series

Writing a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines, or of e^{in\theta}, of whole-number frequencies. On page 3 this is the expansion in eigenfunctions of -d^2/d\theta^2. Wikipedia

Laplacian

The operator \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} in the plane. At each point it is proportional to how far u sits below the average of its values on a small circle around the point. A drumhead’s operator is -c^2\Delta. Wikipedia

Separation of variables

Looking for solutions that are a product of a function of one variable and a function of another, such as u(x, t) = X(x)\,q(t). It splits one equation in several variables into simpler equations in one variable each. Wikipedia

Bessel function

The functions J_m(r) that describe how the modes of a round drum vary from the center to the rim, as sines do along a string. J_0 starts at 1 and swings like a slowly fading cosine, crossing zero at r \approx 2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654, \dots; for m \ge 1, J_m starts at 0. Their zeros, which are not whole-number multiples of the first one, set the drum’s frequencies. Wikipedia, and page 8

Divergence theorem

The total flow out through the boundary of a region equals the sum, over the region, of how much flow is created at each point. It turns forces along the edge of a patch of drumhead into an integral over the patch. Wikipedia

Rayleigh quotient

The ratio of a shape’s stored energy to its mass-weighted size, for example R(f) = \int EI\,(f'')^2\,dx \big/ \int \rho S\,f^2\,dx for a bar; for a shape that meets all the boundary conditions it equals \langle Af, f\rangle/\langle f, f\rangle. Its smallest value, over all nonzero shapes f that obey the conditions at clamped or fixed ends, is the lowest eigenvalue, reached at the lowest mode; in this energy form, conditions at free ends need not be imposed. It explains why removing metal near the base of a reed or tine lowers its pitch and removing it near the tip raises it. Wikipedia

title: Glossary
text:
Shape and spectrum

Weyl’s law

For a drum of area A, the number N(\lambda) of eigenvalues below a large number \lambda is close to A\lambda/4\pi, so the spectrum “hears” the area. A second term, -P\sqrt\lambda/4\pi with P the perimeter, is proved only under extra conditions, but for drums with smooth or polygonal rims the perimeter can be heard anyway, by a smoother count (page 9). Wikipedia

Isospectral

Having the same spectrum, counted with multiplicity. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert found two differently shaped drums that are isospectral. Wikipedia: Hearing the shape of a drum

title: 6 · Change the order
text:
A bar resists bending
The operator. A bar of Young’s modulus E (how stiff the steel is), cross-section area S, second moment of area I (how the cross-section’s shape resists bending) and density \rho obeys 
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S}.
 This is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation. The operator is \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, with four derivatives. Two of them measure how sharply the bar is bent, its curvature u_{xx}; the bar resists bending with a turning effect, the bending moment, proportional to it. Two more turn that into a net force: one derivative turns the change of bending moment along the bar into the sideways force across each cut, the shear force, and another turns the change of shear force along the bar into the net force on each piece.


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MM + dM
      VV + dV
      dx
    
    One slice of the tine. Bending moments (warm), the turning effects that bend it; shear forces (cool), the sideways forces across each cut, push it up and down. Torque balance links them; force balance moves the slice.
  




Step-by-step derivationFrom Newton’s law on a thin slice to four derivatives uses integrals over an area

1. Bending stresses. Bend the bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress, while a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length.

  
  
  
  
  stretched (y > 0)compressed (y < 0)
  neutral axis, y = 0

A fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx} (for a gentle bend, the fraction by which a fiber stretches is its distance from the neutral axis times how fast the bar turns per unit length, which is the curvature u_{xx}), and by Hooke’s law it carries the stress (force per area) \sigma = -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Summed over the cross-section these forces cancel, which is what places the neutral axis through the middle (the centroid) of the cross-section, but their torques do not. They add up to the bending moment 
M = -\int_S y\,\sigma\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_S y^2\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \qquad I = \int_S y^2\,dA ,
 the integrals running over the cross-section. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12; for a round wire of diameter d, I = \pi d^4/64.
2. Shear. A moment rotates a slice but cannot lift it. Each face of a slice also carries a vertical force, the shear force. The conventions: M is the moment on a face that bends the slice into an upward curve, counterclockwise on the right face and clockwise on the left; V is the upward force on the right face, and the left face feels the same force downward.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  MM + dM
  VV + dVdx

We neglect the slice’s resistance to being spun, its rotational inertia, which is accurate when the bar is thin compared with the length of its bending waves; then the torques on the slice must balance. Taking torques about the left face, the shear on the right face times the lever arm dx cancels the change in moment: V\,dx + dM = 0, so V = -M_x.
3. Newton’s law. The vertical forces on the slice do not balance: V(x + dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx accelerates its mass \rho S\,dx. So \rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -M_{xx} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}, the equation above.
What was assumed. Small slopes, a uniform bar, no rotational inertia of the slices (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term that matters only for thick bars and high modes), and no shear deformation of the slices (Timoshenko’s correction).


Boundary conditions. The bending moment is EI\,u_{xx} and the shear force is -EI\,u_{xxx} (the fold derives both). At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: u = 0 and u_x = 0. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a cantilever. At the free tip nothing pushes or bends the bar, so both the moment and the shear force vanish: u_{xx} = 0 and u_{xxx} = 0. That is two conditions at each end, four in all.
Spectrum. Substituting a mode X(x)\cos\omega t into the equation gives \kappa^2 X'''' = \omega^2 X. Write \omega/\kappa = \beta^2, so that X'''' = \beta^4 X; the number \beta plays the role of the string’s wavenumber. Four functions solve this equation: \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions. So X is a combination of the four with four unknown constants. The four boundary conditions are four equations for those constants, and they have a solution other than all zeros exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .
 The roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots, close to (n - \tfrac12)\pi from the second one on. Since \omega \propto \beta^2, the frequency ratios are 
1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots, \qquad \text{growing like } (2n-1)^2 .
 For a string, frequency is proportional to the wavenumber; for a bar, to its square. That change of order spreads the overtones apart, roughly like n^2 instead of n. It does not by itself move them off the whole numbers: with pinned ends, held in place but free to pivot, so u = u_{xx} = 0 at both ends, the shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfy the conditions, four derivatives multiply them by (n\pi/L)^4, and the frequencies are in the ratios 1 : 4 : 9 : 16, all whole numbers. What moves them off is the clamped base and the free tip, which shift the low roots: the first is 1.8751 instead of \pi/2 \approx 1.571, and if every root were exactly (n - \tfrac12)\pi the ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25.



Step-by-step derivationThe four boundary conditions give cos βL cosh βL = −1 uses a 2×2 determinant and integration by parts

The solutions of X'''' = \beta^4X are combinations of \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh and \sinh are the hyperbolic functions, whose fourth derivatives also return them times \beta^4.

Clamped base. X(0) = 0 and X'(0) = 0 leave X = a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x).
Free tip. Differentiating, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the conditions X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read, with the shorthand C_1 = \cos\beta L, S_1 = \sin\beta L, C_2 = \cosh\beta L, S_2 = \sinh\beta L: 
-(C_1 + C_2)\,a - (S_1 + S_2)\,b = 0, \qquad (S_1 - S_2)\,a - (C_1 + C_2)\,b = 0 .

Nonzero solution. Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when ps - qr = 0, the determinant: solve the first for a and substitute into the second. Here 
(C_1 + C_2)^2 + (S_1 + S_2)(S_1 - S_2) = C_1^2 + S_1^2 + 2C_1C_2 + C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 2 + 2C_1C_2 = 0,
 using C_1^2 + S_1^2 = 1 and C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 1. So \cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1.
Roots. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L \approx (n - \tfrac12)\pi, and the approximation improves quickly with n. The first root, 1.8751, is the furthest from it.

The operator d^4/dx^4 with these four conditions is symmetric, by integrating by parts four times (the boundary terms all vanish), so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions perpendicular, as on the circle; with the right domain it is also self-adjoint. Integrating by parts twice gives \int_0^L X\,X''''\,dx = \int_0^L (X'')^2\,dx, so no eigenvalue is negative, and zero is ruled out because X'' = 0 with a clamped base forces X = 0. That is why \beta is a real, positive number.




    Modes of one tine · tap a stem
    
    
    
  

Tuning. Since \beta_1 = 1.8751/L and \omega = \kappa\beta^2, the lowest frequency is f_1 \propto \kappa/L^2 (\propto means “proportional to”), so halving a tine’s free length raises its pitch by a factor of 4, two octaves. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length.
Why it still sounds pitched. Plucked at the tip, a tine starts in the bent shape that a steady push at the tip produces. In that shape the second mode moves only about 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\% as far as the first (fold below). But what you hear is driven by the force the tine puts on the bridge, as on the string page, and for the same displacement a higher mode pushes harder. At the clamp, which in this model is where the tine presses on the bridge, the second mode’s bending moment is about 16% of the first’s and its shear force about 55%. The bridge feels both, so either way the overtone is far stronger in the sound than 2.5% suggests: it is the brief metallic clink of the attack. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. What remains is close to a single frequency, and a sound made of essentially one frequency repeats, so it has a clear pitch.



Step-by-step derivationHow strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode uses integration by parts


The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape u_0, so the bar’s restoring force balances the push.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n c_n X_n, with each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. First, EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n (the mode equation), and the modes are perpendicular, so only the c_n term survives: the integral is \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto u_0, as in the fold above. Inside, EI\,u_0'''' = 0; at the clamp both u_0 and X_n vanish with their slopes; at the tip X_n'' = X_n''' = 0 and u_0'' = 0. The one term left is the tip’s shear force times X_n(L), which is F\,X_n(L). So \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n = F\,X_n(L). This is page 1’s spring again: mode n is a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
Tip values. Taking a = -1 and b = \sigma_n in the fold above gives the standard form X_n = \cosh\beta_nx - \cos\beta_nx - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_nx - \sin\beta_nx), with \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL), about 0.734 and 1.018 for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and its tip value is \pm2 for every n (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and c_2/c_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces. The bending moment at the clamp is EI\,u_{xx} there, and the shear force EI\,u_{xxx} there (up to sign). From the standard form, X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3. Multiplying by c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%.



Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is not perfectly clamped: Chapman models it as clamped at one end, resting on the bridge partway along, and free at the tip, and finds that the measured overtone ratios depend on how the tine’s length is divided by the bridge, which is one reason they spread.

title: 6 · Change the order
text:
What we found
A bar under no tension springs back because it resists bending. Its operator has four derivatives instead of two, so the frequencies spread apart, growing roughly like the square of the mode number. The clamped base and free tip then move them off the whole numbers: 1, 6.27, 17.55, … times the lowest. With pinned ends the same operator would give 1, 4, 9, 16.

title: 6 · Change the order
text:
The next puzzle
A harmonica reed is the same kind of bar, fixed at one end and free at the other, with the same overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times its fundamental. Pluck one and you hear them. Yet a harmonica, blown, plays notes whose overtones are exact whole-number multiples. Where did the bar’s own overtones go?

Watch the wave while you switch between the two. Removing the 220 Hz component changes the wave’s shape, but not how often it repeats: still every 1/220 of a second. The components left are at 440, 660, 880, … Hz, and each of them goes through a whole number of cycles in 1/220 of a second (2, 3, 4, …), so together they still repeat after exactly that time. They do not all fit into 1/440 of a second: 660 Hz would need one and a half cycles. That repetition is what you hear as the pitch. The effect is called the missing fundamental, the fundamental being the component at the repetition rate itself, and it is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over an ordinary telephone line, which cannot carry sounds below about 300 Hz.

title: 0 · What is a note?
section: A note is a pattern that repeats
text:
A note is a pattern that repeats
Sound is air pressure rising and falling. When the pattern repeats every P seconds, with P the shortest such time, you hear a note, and its pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P, measured in hertz, repetitions per second. This holds for repetition rates in the range where we hear pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand times a second; much slower repetition is heard as a rhythm. Middle C, called C4, repeats about 262 times a second.
A pure tone is a single cosine wave, the sound of a tuning fork. Any repeating pattern can be built from pure tones at 1, 2, 3, … times its repetition rate, and from no others; this is Fourier’s theorem, and page 3 shows where it comes from. These tones are its harmonics, and the one at the repetition rate itself is the fundamental. Open “Mix your own” above and try the presets: the wave’s shape changes, and so does the sound’s color, its timbre, but as long as the pattern repeats 220 times a second, the pitch stays put.
In symbols: a pressure signal p(t) is periodic with period P if p(t + P) = p(t) for every t. Any periodic signal that is not too wild (continuous and made of smooth pieces is plenty) is the sum of its Fourier series, 
p(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \cos(2\pi n f t + \phi_n), \qquad f = 1/P .
 The n = 0 term is a constant, the average pressure, usually zero. The possible frequencies nf are fixed by the period alone, and a given sound may use only some of them: a pure tone uses only f. The amplitudes b_n and the phases \phi_n carry everything else about the sound’s shape, and the ear is mostly insensitive to the phases.

title: 0 · What is a note?
text:
Why whole numbers matter
Turn it around. If an object vibrates at several frequencies at once, its sound repeats only when those frequencies are whole-number multiples of one common frequency. For two tones, that means their frequency ratio is a fraction j/k of whole numbers, in lowest terms; the pattern then repeats every k cycles of the lower tone. Only a small k gives a repetition fast enough to hear as one pitch. Try it:


  2 : 13 : 21.59 : 1 (a drum)Play
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, it lines up only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch.





ProofTwo tones repeat together exactly when their frequency ratio is rational

Let s(t) = \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) with 0 < f_1 < f_2.
If the ratio is rational, s is periodic. Write f_2/f_1 = j/k in lowest terms and put P = k/f_1. Then f_1P = k and f_2P = j are whole numbers, so both cosines return to their starting values after time P, and s(t+P) = s(t).
If s is periodic, the ratio is rational. Suppose s(t+P) = s(t) for all t, with P > 0. At t = 0 this gives s(P) = s(0) = 2. A sum of two cosines equals 2 only when both cosines equal 1, so \cos(2\pi f_1P) = \cos(2\pi f_2P) = 1, which means f_1P and f_2P are whole numbers. So f_2/f_1 = (f_2P)/(f_1P) is a ratio of whole numbers. Since f_2/f_1 = j/k, we have k\,(f_2P) = j\,(f_1P), so k divides j\,(f_1P); as j and k share no factor, k divides the whole number f_1P. So every period is a multiple of k/f_1, and k/f_1 is the shortest one.
The shortest period k/f_1 grows with the denominator k. A ratio like 1.59 = 159/100 is rational, but its pattern repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly for the ear to hear as one pitch. How the ear decides what counts as “simple enough” is a question of perception, not mathematics; see pitch.





Reader questionIs a musical note one frequency?

No. A note is a sound whose pressure repeats every P seconds, and its pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P. By the Fourier series above, its components can only be at f, 2f, 3f, \dots, and usually several are present at once. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not a component at f itself is present, and the weights b_n set the timbre: a piano C4 and a violin C4 share f and differ in their b_n. So a note corresponds to a period, not to a single frequency.

title: 0 · What is a note?
text:
What we found
A note is a sound that repeats. Its pitch is how often it repeats, and so one note is a sum of tones at whole-number multiples of that rate.

title: 0 · What is a note?
text:
The next puzzle
So a clear note needs frequencies at exact whole-number multiples of one frequency. A guitar string is just a piece of wire, and a drumhead just a sheet of plastic. Why would the wire vibrate at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times one frequency, and the drumhead not? To find out, start with the simplest thing that vibrates at all: one mass on a spring.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text: Using a few examples, we demonstrate how to conditionally break out of nested for loop using for-else clause.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: finished
Layer 1 for i = 1: start
  1 0
  1 1
  1 2
  Layer 2 for i = 1: finished
Layer 1 for i = 2: start
  2 0
  2 1


Here, no continue in the else part. Thus, the program breaks unconditionally after finishing its job in the i==0 round.

for i in range(4):
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3):
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> the for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: completed")
    break # always reached at i = 0

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: completed
